articles.title: Lucid Dream Control: Mechanisms, Challenges, and Future Directions
articles.abstract: Lucid dreaming (LD) is the phenomenon during which dreamers are aware they are dreaming and may be able to influence dream content. Dream manipulation, or dream control, plays a critical role in the applications of LD across both clinical and non-clinical domains and may be a key determinant of therapeutic success. However, not all lucid dreamers are able to effectively influence their dreams, and achieving dream lucidity does not automatically translate into meaningful control. Despite the growing interest in LD, research on the mechanisms, reliability, and effectiveness of dream manipulation remains limited. This work critically reviews the current state of research on dream manipulation within LD, identifies gaps in knowledge, and proposes future directions for addressing challenges in reliably controlling lucid dreams. We begin by exploring the elements of dreams that can be influenced through dream manipulation (including dream environment, body, and narrative) and discuss strategies, challenges, and individual differences in dream control. Additionally, we explore the clinical and non-clinical applications of manipulating lucid dreams and call for future research that focuses on standardizing dream control assessment methods, empirical studies evaluating dream manipulation strategies, and a deeper understanding of the cognitive, emotional, and neurophysiological factors that contribute to successful dream manipulation. Finally, the Lucid Dream Control General (LDC-G) and Lucid Dream Control for Specific Experiences (LDC-SE) scales are proposed as new standardized methods to evaluate dream control during LD. These questionnaires provide individual scores for specific aspects of LD control and overall dream control proficiency.

articles.title: Experimental Evidence on the Effect of Mixed-Mode Survey Designs on Item Measurement and Variable Correlations
articles.authors: Liam Wright, Georgia D Tomova, Matt Brown, Konstantinos G. Tsigaridis, Morag Henderson, Richard J. Silverwood
articles.abstract: Background: Mixed-mode designs can generate bias in all types of analysis of survey data due to systematic differences in how survey participants may respond according to mode – a phenomenon referred to as a mode effect. There is widespread evidence of mode effects upon item measurement (e.g., item means and proportions), but less on associations between survey items, despite estimating associations being a primary use of survey data. Methods: We estimated average differences (means and proportions) in item responses according to mode using data from an experiment in which participants were randomized to respond via web questionnaire, video interview, or in-person interview. We then used these estimates to simulate (counterfactual) data from two web-then-in-person sequential mixed-mode surveys of young adults in the United Kingdom (Next Steps and the Millennium Cohort Study, MCS) as if they were collected using a single mode, web. We estimated associations between variables using this simulated data and compared these against associations obtained using the observed (i.e., factual) data; the difference between the two provides a measure of variation in variable correlations reflecting the mixed-mode survey design. Results: Mode effects were observed for an array of items comparing web with in-person and video modes; differences between video and in-person were more muted. Participants in web were more likely to report negatively valent values for sensitive items, in particular (e.g., poorer physical and mental health, lower life satisfaction, and greater financial difficulty), though effect sizes were generally small with few exceeding 0.2 SD and all below 0.3 SD. The impact of mode effects on variable associations in the mixed-mode surveys was also generally small: a 0.004 SD change in absolute effect sizes on average in both Next Steps and the MCS. Conclusion: Items related to sensitive characteristics showed small mode effects when comparing web and in-person or video interview modes. Mode effects did not appear to translate into substantial changes to associations between variables as assessed in a sequential web-then-in-person mixed-mode survey compared with a counterfactual web-only survey.

articles.title: From international dissemination to encountering epistemic diversity: communication about art and the art of communication in the Comprehensive Collection of Ancient Chinese paintings.
articles.abstract: This paper reconceptualizes the international dissemination of A Comprehensive Collection of Ancient Chinese Paintings (the Series) not merely as cultural transmission or global circulation, but as an epistemic practice of exchange that transcends disciplinary, professional, and geographical, and cultural boundaries. Drawing on perspectives from communication science, intercultural exchange, and art–science interaction, the paper examines how dissemination functions as an epistemic practice that both translates and generates knowledge. First, it situates art communication and dissemination as a site of knowledge creation and epistemic encounter rather than a passive transfer of information to audiences (communicating about art). Second, it argues that the Series enables epistemic innovation and diversity through the interaction between multiple, heterogeneous knowledge practices, facilitated by cross-cultural dialogue and inter- and transdisciplinary exchange. Finally, it discusses the interactive and engaging dissemination practices through which the Series is translated to broader audiences, focusing on experiential, sensory, and narrative forms of engagement in immersive exhibitions and digital media platforms (the art of communication). The paper argues that a significant value of the Series lies in its capacity to function as an epistemic infrastructure: one that not only transmits and circulates knowledge on Chinese art and cultural heritage, but also enables encounters between different ways of knowing and, as a result, generates new forms of understanding and epistemic diversity.

articles.title: Conclusion: reflections on and conditions for meaningful art-science interaction
articles.abstract: This conclusion brings together the diverse reflections on meaningful art–science interactions that have emerged throughout the chapters, exploring key takeaways from each contribution. It presents a colorful palette of disciplinary, professional, and artistic perspectives, showing how different ways of knowing meet, contrast, and resonate, while highlighting experiences, insights, emerging practices, and recurring questions across the volume. This journey of discovery through varied perspectives and topics culminates in an outline of possible future directions, not as prescriptions or a manual, but as invitations for readers to explore new pathways beyond the scope of this book, and to embark on further journeys of encounter, co-creation, and epistemic exchange.

articles.title: Working across and beyond boundaries: a journey in art – science collaborations
articles.abstract: This chapter, written in the form of a dialogue, features an in-depth interview with professor Johan Wagemans, a renowned perception researcher and principal investigator of the Palettes project. Over nearly two decades, Wagemans has been at the forefront of interdisciplinary research bridging science and art. In this conversation, he reflects on his personal journey working with artists across disciplinary boundaries and explores how his understanding of art–science relationships has transformed from his earliest collaboration (Parallellepipeda in 2008) to his current work in Palettes. Through a series of anecdotes and critical reflections, the chapter highlights both the strengths and the challenges of conducting long-term art–science collaborations. Wagemans discusses what has worked, what has not, and why, offering insights into the subtle dynamics of interdisciplinary exchange and the conditions that foster meaningful interaction. Looking ahead, he considers emerging pathways, ambitions, and opportunities for future art–science engagement, particularly beyond formal academic structures. The chapter is complemented by selected artworks that symbolize key turning points in his journey and visually illustrate themes raised in the dialogue. Together, the narrative and visual materials illuminate how art–science collaborations can evolve, deepen, and open new directions for research and creative practice.

articles.title: A practical guide to perform an Interdisciplinary Scoping Review
articles.abstract: The growth of interdisciplinary research has brought with it an increasing demand for robust methods to map and synthesize diverse bodies of evidence. Among these, scoping reviews have emerged as a particularly valuable tool. They allow researchers to systematically explore complex, cross-cutting topics, clarify definitions, identify gaps, and build foundations for future inquiry. This guide was developed to respond to that need. It provides a step-by-step framework for conducting an interdisciplinary scoping review, illustrated with the example of digitalisation and its effects on the physical health of older workers. By walking through each stage of the process—from formulating research questions to reporting and publishing findings—the guide aims to make the methodology transparent, practical, and replicable for researchers at different career stages and across disciplines. The approach presented here is rooted in established frameworks and aligned with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines to ensure rigour and clarity. At the same time, it reflects the lessons learned from my own experience conducting interdisciplinary reviews in practice. I hope this guide encourages researchers to approach scoping reviews in a more systematic and transparent way, while also fostering collaboration across disciplines.

articles.title: Beyond technical thinking: revealing reflections on technology, media art, logocentrism, and epistemic diversity

subjects.name: Social and Philosophical Foundations of Education

articles.abstract: This chapter examines art–science-technology interactions and epistemic diversity in a world shaped by technological progress and scientific knowledge, which are deeply intertwined. While technology is often understood as the use and development of instruments, a means to an end, it is not only something we use; it also shapes how we understand and engage with reality. In this technological ‘revealing’ of reality, the world increasingly presents itself as measurable, controllable, and exploitable: as a resource. This chapter refers to this instrumentalization of reality as technical thinking. In this chapter, we first show that within artistic practice, the use of technology does not necessarily lead to technical thinking. When engaged within artistic practice, it can open non-technical, contemplative ways of relating to the world. The chapter then reverses this perspective by showing that technical thinking can also operate without visible machines, particularly through logocentric language in scientific practice, where articulation and description function as a technology of ordering and control and become conditions for what counts as knowledge. Ultimately, the chapter asks how artistic and other ways of knowing can enter scientific contexts without being assimilated into technical thinking, and reflects on the conditions for sustaining epistemic diversity in contemporary knowledge institutions.

articles.title: Meritocracy, Legitimation and Belonging on the University of Cambridge’s Foundation Year
articles.abstract: Widening participation spans the whole student lifecycle, from access through to success within higher education and progression beyond it, yet policy and evaluation have concentrated on the access stage alone. Far less is known about how students admitted through widened access routes come to understand the legitimacy of their place once inside an elite university. Reporting twenty-one (n=21) walking interviews with students who entered the University of Cambridge through its Foundation Year, a one-year pre-degree programme for applicants whose educational opportunities have been constrained by structural disadvantage, this article examines a tension at the heart of meritocracy. Participants recognized that admissions standards are shaped by unequal opportunity, though the recognition appeared not to weaken their commitment to meritocratic judgement, and they endeavored to suffuse their belonging with proof of deservingness. Such a pattern sits uneasily with Bourdieusian accounts of symbolic domination grounded in misrecognition, and points towards a compliance sustained through lucid perception of meritocracy and its ideological demands. Analysis of the walks suggests that the route organizes this tension by marking students publicly as different, by tying belonging to a competitive progression threshold, by collapsing heterogeneous experiences into a single administrative category, and by locating institutional judgement in everyday encounters with teaching staff. Belonging emerges less as a settled outcome of admission than as a conditional status that must be repeatedly earned. Widening access may therefore secure entry without securing the later stages of participation, so long as the legitimacy of membership continues to be organized through meritocratic evaluation that students simultaneously critique and reproduce.

articles.title: Cognitive and Proactive Building Operation: Current Status and an Eight-Gap Research Agenda
articles.abstract: Buildings dominate final energy demand, but operation remains reactive. This paper reviews cognitive and proactive building operation and derives a research agenda. Two questions guide the analysis: RQ1, the current status of seven constituent streams; RQ2, the gaps explaining the persistent distance between concept and practice. A critical review (July 2026) covers cognitive building concepts, MPC, RL/data-driven control, OCC, AFDD, cognitive digital twins with semantic infrastructure, and LLM-based agentic systems. Retrieval prioritised recent reviews and field deployments, with snowballing. An explicit evidence hierarchy and gap-derivation rule are stated, and bibliographic records were verified against metadata. An independent bibliometric strand uses a documented Web of Science query on cognitive, adaptive, cybernetic, and AI vocabulary, yielding 113 records (2011-2026). This corpus is profiled bibliometrically and mapped onto the gap taxonomy. The query string is reproduced verbatim, its retrieval behaviour is audited, and two artefacts materially affecting interpretation are discussed. The status pattern is consistent: conceptually rich, simulation-mature, field-poor. Bibliometrics sharpen this: 49% of records are from 2024-2026; a single 2020 review accounts for 49% of citations; only 20% are building-related (rest in software, manufacturing, general digital twins); cybernetic-building intersections contain only three records, the latest from 2015; co-word analysis reveals structural zeros, with cybernetics and self-adaptive systems never co-occurring. The query audit confirms: although the viable system model is named, exactly one of 113 records engages Beer's model, and it does not concern buildings. Outside the database, this organizing principle is applied in production management, software architecture, and agentic AI, but not in contemporary building operation. Eight gaps are derived: G1 definitional/theoretical, G2 reactive-to-proactive practice, G3 simulation-to-reality, G4 fragmentation, G5 architectural mechanism, G6 evaluation, G7 longevity/resilience, and G8 human factors/governance. G1-G4 and G6-G8 restate explicit deficits; G5 is an interpretive synthesis. The paper argues G5, the absence of an organizing principle for allocating sensing, computation, and actuation across subsystems, spatial scales, and time horizons, is structurally prior to several other gaps, and candidate principles are compared. Contributions include a cross-stream status consolidation, an evidence-anchored gap taxonomy with derivation rules, bibliometric quantitative support, and a defended keystone-gap argument. The review is evaluative rather than exhaustive and positions its findings as an evidence-based hypothesis set for a subsequent protocol-driven systematic review.

articles.title: Is Entrepreneurship Legitimate Where the State Is Not? Insights from Machine Learning Methods
articles.abstract: Does the political environment influence people’s perceptions of entrepreneurship? Should there be any correlation between state legitimacy and that of entrepreneurship? These questions are crucial, as the success of any developmental tool, including entrepreneurship, depends on its public approval. To find the answers, the present paper examines Iran as an extreme case of a state facing recurring episodes of legitimacy crisis while simultaneously deeply involved in promoting entrepreneurship and penetrating the entrepreneurial ecosystem. The paper reveals that Iranians’ perceptions of entrepreneurship essentially mirror the polarized political atmosphere in society, divided between those who support the country’s entrepreneurial achievements and those who challenge them. Nonetheless, pragmatic reasons, rather than anti-state emotions, such as the state’s problematic intervention in the ecosystem, fueled these criticisms. More crucially, the paper contributes to the literature on institutional determinants of entrepreneurship legitimacy by demonstrating a direct and meaningful association between state and entrepreneurship legitimacy.

articles.title: Energy Security vs. Food Inflation: An Empirical Analysis of Crop-Substitution and Price Spillover Effects in India's E20 Ethanol Expansion
articles.abstract: India's Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP) Programme has advanced from a marginal 1.14–1.53 per cent blending rate in 2013–14 to the statutory 20 per cent (E20) target by Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) 2025–26, five years ahead of the original 2030 deadline set under the National Policy on Biofuels, 2018. This rapid scale-up has been accompanied by an equally rapid structural shift in feedstock composition: official data show the share of grain-based ethanol (maize, rice, and damaged food grain) rising from roughly 9 per cent of total procurement in ESY 2020–21 to nearly 60 per cent by early ESY 2024–25, with industry-association estimates placing maize's individual share alone at approximately 50 per cent by ESY 2024–25, up from 6.2 per cent two years earlier. This paper examines the resulting energy-security-versus-food-inflation trade-off using officially reported and peer-reviewed data. It synthesises the National Policy on Biofuels (2018, amended 2022), the NITI Aayog Roadmap for Ethanol Blending in India 2020–25, Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas (MoPNG) blending statistics, USDA Foreign Agricultural Service (FAS) maize market data, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and Ministry of Finance inflation reporting, and a 2026 peer-reviewed partial-equilibrium modelling study (published in PLOS One by researchers at the Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad, the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, and the FABLE Consortium). The analysis finds credible evidence of crop-substitution pressure — a 14.7 per cent year-on-year decline in maize production coinciding with record consumption, an 84 per cent collapse in maize exports, and open-market maize prices exceeding the government's minimum support price by approximately 11 per cent in April 2024 — alongside documented cumulative energy-security gains of over ₹1.36–1.59 lakh crore in foreign exchange savings. However, the paper finds that a direct, India-specific econometric (VAR/Granger) estimate of ethanol-to-food-price transmission does not yet exist in the peer-reviewed literature; this study is accordingly framed as a literature- and data-grounded empirical synthesis rather than primary econometric estimation, and it explicitly flags this gap as a priority for future research. Policy recommendations centre on feedstock diversification toward 2G/cellulosic ethanol, protection of grain buffer stocks, and integration of food-price monitoring into the biofuel roadmap.

articles.title: Validation of the Tolerance of Surroundings Scale and Autonomy Scale among People with Long-Term Care Needs
articles.authors: Takazumi Ono, Hiroko Costantini, Shinichiro Kumagaya, Ikuko Sugawara, Katsuya Iijima, Misato Nihei

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Social relationships with surrounding people and an individual's autonomy are fundamental components of age-friendly community and long-term care (LTC). The objective of the present study was to evaluate the psychometric properties of the Tolerance of Surroundings Scale (TSS) and Autonomy Scales (AS) among people with LTC needs. We distributed a self-administered questionnaire to four daycare/day-services facilities and three home-visit nurse stations in Japan. The TSS consists of 20 items under 4 factors and the AS includes 20 items based on 3 factors. These scales were previously validated in the Japanese general population. 259 people participated in the survey. Confirmatory factor analysis demonstrated model fit for the TSS was good, whereas that for the AS was acceptable. In addition, explanatory factor analysis demonstrated that the AS had 2-factor structure specified for people with LTC. The regression coefficients for subjective well-being were 0.43 (95%CI 0.23, 0.62) and 0.73 (95%CI 0.50, 0.96), respectively. The alphas in the TSS and the AS ranged from 0.75 to 0.88, from 0.53 to 0.91, respectively. The alphas of the AS in first and second factors specified for people with LTC needs were 0.91 and 0.70, respectively. In conclusion, the TSS and the AS were valid and reliable in people with LTC needs. However, regarding the AS, different factor structures should be used (the structure in general population and that specified in people with LTC needs) depending on the purpose of the assessment. In addition, further studies to assess test-retest reliability and measurement error are needed.

articles.title: Von Neumann’s Blurry Elephant: On The Need for Care and Clarity in Modeling Complex Social Systems
articles.abstract: Wildman and Shults have laid out an ambitious scope for their book, Modeling Religion: Simulating the Transformation of Worldviews, Lifeways, and Civilization. I laud their aims and echo their enthusiasm for modeling. However, I also believe that Wildman and Shults largely fail to achieve their goals. Their models are neither clear nor well justified, and so their results are not compelling. The book’s value is in the attempt, and in the discussions which are based more on interpretations of empirical data than on conclusions from the published models. I believe it will be instructive to explain why I think the goals of the book were not achieved. To do so, I will first explain a bit about how the models work. I will then discuss general guidelines for the use of formal models to understand complex social dynamics, and how Wildman Shults fail to meet them.

articles.title: Resilience: Understand Breakdown, Foster Recovery, and Choose the Right Perspective

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Resilience denotes the capacity of a system to withstand shocks and to recover from them. We distinguish between two different types of dynamics. The first allows for a separation between phases of normalcy and phases of rapid breakdown followed by slow recovery. The second applies to volatile organizations in which such phases are intertwined. Breakdown is often self-inflicted. Situation awareness is impaired by psychological mechanisms that lead to incorrect expectations regarding societal dynamics. Through positive feedback, the failure of a few elements is amplified into a failure cascade. However, positive feedback can also be harnessed to enable recovery. In volatile systems, resilience must be understood as an emergent property arising from the interaction of agents. This necessitates a data-driven approach to inform agent-based models, drawing on repositories, knowledge graphs, or tools from artificial intelligence. Such models help demonstrate that resilience represents a compromise between robustness and adaptivity. Maximizing performance frequently comes at the expense of resilience, and second-order solutions aimed at transforming the system prove more promising than attempts to reconstruct past conditions.

articles.title: Varieties of democratic vulnerability: a comparative study of checks and balances and popular acceptance of transgressions
articles.authors: Honorata Mazepus, Magnus Feldmann, Giovanni D'Agostino
articles.abstract: The recent wave of democratic backsliding has demonstrated that liberal democracies are vulnerable to subversion by authoritarian leaders. Research showed that democratically elected leaders remove checks and balances that constrain their power. One of the explanations why leaders can violate democratic rules focuses on the response of citizens who trade off democracy for partisan and policy gains. This article investigates cross-country differences in vulnerabilities to democratic backsliding by comparing democratic priority profiles of citizens and the patterns of approval for transgressions of democratic rules. We use observational evidence from online surveys with large quota-based samples of citizens in a two-party presidential system (USA, N > 1700), a multi-party parliamentary system based on proportional representation with some semi-presidential features (Poland, N >1800), and a consociational parliamentary system based on proportional representation (Netherlands, N = > 2100). To complement observational evidence, we test experimentally some of these aggregate-level differences: next to partisanship and policy gains, we also manipulate different democratic transgressions (protest rights and decree powers) and measure their effects on government approval in the three countries. Our results show that citizens of different countries have different democratic priority profiles and differ in their disapproval of specific transgressions. Although overall transgressions are not rewarded, and citizens are mostly vigilant and disapproving of violating democratic rules, we find both observational and experimental evidence indicating that liberal democracies can have different vulnerabilities that relate to the democratic attitudes of citizens.

articles.title: Catch the Patient, Not the AI: Collective Sensemaking in an Online Health Community
articles.abstract: Patients and caregivers increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) tools to interpret medical reports, weigh care decisions, and seek emotional support. Yet most research treats patient-facing AI as a private exchange between a user and a system, leaving open how AI-related content is taken up once users carry it back into the peer communities where they already make sense of illness. This study examines collective sensemaking around AI in House086, China's largest online community for lymphoma patients and caregivers. We identified roughly 400 publicly accessible discussion threads (2014 to 2026) through AI-related keyword searches and manual screening, extracted them into structured case profiles using a schema-prompted large language model (Claude Sonnet 4.6, deployed via AWS Bedrock), and conducted mixed-method analysis. After quality control, the verified analytic sample comprised 337 post-ChatGPT records focused on widespread conversational-AI use. Members most often reported using AI for informational support, followed by second opinions and psychosocial support. Although members often introduced AI favorably, roughly one in six described feeling overwhelmed by AI output. When other members responded, they frequently engaged the poster's underlying medical or emotional intent while leaving the AI dimension unaddressed. The tendency to bypass AI persisted even in threads seeking triangulation between AI output and other information sources, and when posters shared overwhelmed or unfavorable experiences with AI. On the occasions when members did discuss the AI, they were more often cautious than endorsing. Rather than auditing AI output for factual accuracy, the community more often worked to deflate the false certainty it produced, placing a single AI answer back among multiple sources of judgment. This study argues that AI does not replace the interpretive work of online health communities, nor is it systematically audited by them. Instead, it shifts the locus of sensemaking downstream, so that the community continues to catch the person even when it does not catch the AI, and the interpretive authority that follows does not settle in any single place. We discuss implications for CSCW theory, online-community norms, and patient-facing AI design.

articles.title: Full Reporting in Empirical Asset Pricing: A Statistical Decision-Theoretic Approach
articles.abstract: This study develops a full-reporting framework for empirical asset pricing grounded in statistical decision theory. In the abductive stage, simulated pseudo-factor model spaces are used to evaluate whether candidate test scores can distinguish valid from invalid model states through likelihood behavior, receiver operating characteristic analysis, and classification metrics. In the inductive stage, realized sample scores are mapped to likelihood ratios, error rates, and decision criteria, translating observed evidence into model-state predictions. Reporting this complete inferential chain enables test performance and realized evidence to be integrated into transparent assessments of factor-model validity.

articles.title: Brechas de observabilidad en la vigilancia del riesgo psicosocial laboral en América Latina: fundamentos para una arquitectura dinámica con evidencia desde Chile
articles.abstract: Periodic psychosocial risk assessment systems share a limitation that is architectural rather than psychometric: the aggregation function that produces the organizational indicator irreversibly destroys spatial information about the state of the internal units composing it, regardless of instrument quality or measurement frequency. This paper reports a simulation study with empirical calibration that tests four confirmatory hypotheses, declared a priori, using an agent-based model formalized under the ODD 2020 protocol and calibrated with CEAL-SM 2023 data (N=768,505 Chilean workers). The model demonstrates that concentrated deterioration in a minority of organizational units produces a Spatial Dilution Ratio of up to 4.11×, rendering it either fully invisible (existential gap) or detectable but unlocalizable (granularity gap) to periodic aggregate assessment, while uniformly distributed deterioration produces convergence between architectures — confirming by inversion that the gap is spatial, not temporal. This paper proposes DYNOR (Dynamic Organizational Risk Surveillance Framework) to occupy the follow-up step of the standard five-step preventive cycle in Latin America, operating continuously between periodic assessment anchors rather than replacing them. The framework is directly relevant for normative systems in Chile, Colombia, Mexico, Peru, Argentina, Uruguay, and Brazil.

articles.title: The Changing Role of Major Stakeholders: A Review of Publisher, Vendor, and Institutional Adaptation in the Scholarly Communication Ecosystem
articles.abstract: This article reviews the changing roles of major stakeholders in the scholarly communication ecosystem, focusing on publishers, vendors, and academic institutions. The rapid growth of digital technologies, open access initiatives, and evolving researcher expectations have significantly transformed traditional scholarly communication practices. Through a critical review of existing literature, this study examines how these stakeholders redefine their responsibilities and adopt adaptation strategies to remain relevant in a dynamic academic environment. The analysis highlights key strategies such as business model innovation, service redesign, policy reform, and technological integration as central to effective adaptation. The findings indicate that publishers increasingly function as service providers, vendors play a vital role in technological infrastructure and analytics, and institutions adopt more active roles in research dissemination and support. This review concludes that sustained collaboration and continuous adaptation among publishers, vendors, and institutions are essential for developing an efficient, accessible, and sustainable scholarly communication ecosystem.

articles.title: A Certification Gate for Emerging-Topic Detection: Pre-Registration, Negative Controls, and a Second-Domain Transfer Test on arXiv
articles.abstract: Methods for detecting emerging research topics keep multiplying, but they are rarely validated against ground truth chosen independently of the method: most are assessed on internal coherence or a few hand-picked success stories. This paper contributes not a new detector but a certification gate, a pre-registered, negative-controlled validation protocol any emergence detector can be run through. Before results are seen, the gate fixes (i) a binary "flagged rising" criterion, (ii) an externally-sourced positive set and a matched negative-control set, and (iii) Wilson-95% reporting of recall, specificity and precision. Applied to the temporal component of a five-dimension emergence system over arXiv stat.ML (2018–2023; 76 topics), the gate yields recall 93% (14/15, Wilson 95% [70,99]) and specificity 100% (13/13, [77,100]). The identical protocol is then run on a second, structurally different domain (arXiv cs.CR; 2018–2023; 129 topics) under a benchmark frozen and timestamped before scoring. This is a transfer test, not a replication: with only two domains it characterises how the protocol behaves out-of-corpus, not whether the first result reproduces. Recall falls to 62% (10/16, [39,82]) and specificity to 69% (9/13, [42,87]); pooled, recall is 77% (24/31, [60,89]) and specificity 85% (22/26, [66,94]). The intervals are wide by construction: at these n the benchmark is underpowered to rank detectors and demonstrates only the gate. The honest degradation is the point: a validation that reported 100% on one corpus and hid the second would be the overfitting it claims to detect. The protocol, both benchmarks with timestamp proofs, and a disclosed pre-scoring amendment are released, and the gate's numbers are reported with and without that amendment.

articles.title: Reconstructing Sexual Economy: The role of Women in the subsistence of Sex Work and Tourism and the Rise of Single Mothers in The Philippines
articles.abstract: This paper examines the Philippine sexual economy through a structural sociological and historical lens, arguing that commercial sex work is not merely an outcome of individual choice or moral failure but a rational adaptation to intersecting historical, economic, and institutional constraints. Drawing upon interdisciplinary literature from sociology, history, gender studies, public policy, and human rights, the study traces the evolution of the Philippine sexual economy from Spanish colonial rule and the institutionalization of prostitution around American military bases to its contemporary integration within global tourism. It demonstrates how persistent poverty, gender-segmented labor markets, discriminatory employment practices, and inadequate social welfare systems have made sex work a significant strategy of female household subsistence. The paper further examines how these structural conditions contribute to the growth of solo motherhood and the enduring marginalization of Amerasian children abandoned by foreign military personnel and tourists. It argues that the coexistence of criminalization, anti-trafficking legislation, and external geopolitical influence has produced a policy framework that simultaneously punishes, victimizes, and silences sex workers while denying them labor rights and limiting effective public health interventions. Rather than framing prostitution solely as a criminal justice or moral issue, the analysis situates it within broader systems of political economy, gender inequality, and postcolonial governance. The paper concludes by proposing evidence-based structural reforms, including labor market expansion, strengthened support for solo mothers, rights-based legal reform, and greater accountability for the historical legacies of foreign military intervention. By reframing the Philippine sexual economy as a structural rather than individual phenomenon, this study contributes to broader debates on gender, labor, postcolonial development, and the sociology of informal economies.

articles.title: The Precarious Center: Structural Vulnerability and the Economic Squeeze of South Asia’s Lower Middle Class
articles.abstract: This paper examines the lower middle class in South Asia as a structurally vulnerable “missing middle” caught between extreme poverty and genuine income security. It argues that conventional middle-class definitions often obscure the fragility of households that earn too much to qualify for targeted welfare yet too little to access private health care, quality education, or reliable financial protection. Drawing on evidence from India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, and West Bengal, the paper shows how this group is squeezed by informal employment, exclusion from social protection, catastrophic out-of-pocket health costs, rising education expenses, regressive taxation, inflation, and debt dependence. It also highlights how remittances, asset ownership, and consumer goods can create a false impression of security while masking deep exposure to economic shocks. The paper concludes that although the extreme poor remain the most deprived in absolute terms, the lower middle class is arguably the most systemically neglected and precariously positioned segment in South Asia, trapped in a cycle of permanent vulnerability without a stable path to upward mobility.

articles.title: Equal Protection or Conceptual Conformity? Global Gender Governance, Norm Translation and Cultural Sovereignty
articles.abstract: Global gender governance has expanded from instruments centred on women’s legal equality and protection from sex-based discrimination to a heterogeneous field encompassing gender mainstreaming, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, sexuality education, institutional inclusion and gender-transformative programming. This article asks when such expansion represents legitimate human-rights protection and when transnational norm transfer risks becoming conceptual conformity. It combines a critical integrative review of 42 scholarly works with structured analysis of 29 primary policy instruments issued by global, regional and national institutions. Searches were conducted through five pre-specified OpenAlex queries and reported using a PRISMA-adapted, transparently bounded design. The analysis distinguishes a universal protection floor, context-dependent institutional measures and contested anthropological propositions. It finds no evidence of a single, centrally coordinated global command structure. It does identify polycentric conceptual expansion, soft-law diffusion, donor and reputational leverage, and forms of localisation whose practical openness varies considerably. Global norms have provided indispensable resources against violence, exclusion and sex-based inequality; they can also blur the boundary between protecting persons and requiring assent to disputed accounts of sex, identity, embodiment and family. The article develops a fifteen-test Conceptual Sovereignty and Gender Governance Framework to assess dignity, safety, evidence, authority, participation, translation, non-compulsion, proportionality, women’s rights, minority protection, conscience, democratic legitimacy, conditionality and reviewability. Equal dignity, it argues, requires robust protection without making conceptual uniformity the price of civic inclusion.

articles.title: Introduction: a palette of meaningful art-science interactions
articles.abstract: This introductory chapter frames the central question guiding the volume: what makes an art–science interaction meaningful? It outlines how this guiding question emerged within the PALETTES research environment, an inter- and transdisciplinary project that brings together researchers from different backgrounds, artists, and cultural practitioners in collaborative exchanges within and beyond academia. Recognizing that art-science interactions are multifaceted and context-dependent, the book explores meaningfulness through different disciplinary and practice-based perspectives. Against this background, the chapter positions the book within ongoing debates on art–science collaboration and epistemic diversity, and situates its scope, rationale, and distinctive features in relation to the current state of the art (and science). It discusses the positioning of art as an epistemic practice in its own right as central to the book’s approach, critically addressing the risk of instrumentalization when art is reduced to serving as a tool for predefined scientific goals. The book examines how art and science can enrich one another as distinct yet interacting ways of knowing. The chapter also reflects on the collaborative conditions under which the chapters were developed, showing how they emerged through sustained dialogue, co-creative activities, and iterative exchange. The contributions thus reflect the very collaborative processes they seek to examine at a meta-level. The chapter further clarifies its intended audiences and concludes with a reflection on the approach to composing the book, including the principles that guided the selection and development of the contributions, as well as on the composition and structure of the book itself, explaining how the volume is organized without fixed thematic divisions, and how this structuring can be understood as a curatorial practice that makes visible the relations between contributions. It also provides a brief overview of the chapters and their respective lenses, followed by cross-chapter connections that offer orientation for navigating the volume as a whole.

articles.title: The Halo of Presentation: A Six-Month Autoethnographic Case Study of Self-Presentation, Peer Perception, and Social Evaluation Among Adolescent Peers
articles.abstract: Human beings continually evaluate one another using observable cues such as appearance, clothing, grooming, posture, confidence, and interpersonal behavior. These evaluations frequently dictate the trajectory of social interactions long before substantial verbal communication occurs. Although psychological research has extensively examined first impressions and interpersonal perception in controlled laboratory settings, comparatively few qualitative studies explore how deliberate alterations in self-presentation influence everyday social dynamics within an established adolescent peer group over an extended longitudinal period. This six-month qualitative autoethnographic case study (January–June 2026) investigates these dynamics within a naturally occurring secondary school environment. Acting simultaneously as researcher and participant within a stable core friendship group, I systematically modified outward self-presentation across two equal, contrasting phases. Phase One (January–March) established a baseline characterized by disciplined grooming, regular exercise, curated clothing, confident posture, and low approval-seeking behavior. Phase Two (April–June) introduced deliberate reductions in grooming, repetitive clothing usage, unmaintained hair growth, lower social confidence, and heightened people-pleasing behaviors. Digital field notes documented everyday interactions. Qualitative thematic comparison revealed marked shifts: Phase One corresponded with higher perceived respect, frequent social invitations, and sustained conversational engagement. Conversely, Phase Two corresponded with increased teasing, social distancing, and diminished conversational engagement, with shifts becoming noticeable 11–17 days post-modification. These findings are analyzed through established sociopsychological frameworks, including the Halo Effect, Impression Management, Expectancy Violations Theory, and Status Characteristics Theory. While acknowledging the inherent limitations of a single-subject autoethnographic design, this study provides a transparent lived account demonstrating how outward presentation actively negotiates adolescent peer evaluation.

articles.title: THE FORMATION OF THE U.S. HEGEMONIC REVOLUTIONARY BLOC
articles.abstract: This article examines the formation and transformation of the revolutionary hegemonic bloc in colonial America during the period 1763-1776. Drawing on Antonio Gramsci's theory of hegemony, the analysis conceptualizes the American Revolution as a process of formation of class alliances among heterogeneous social classes under conditions of crisis. The article argues that revolutionary unity did not emerge spontaneously nor through elite manipulation alone, but through a prolonged and conflictual process in which merchants, large landowners, and lawyers articulated a hegemonic project capable of incorporating artisans and yeomen, while simultaneously containing popular radicalism. Using a structural-historical approach, the article distinguishes between two phases of the revolutionary crisis: an initial phase characterized by a fragmented and decentralized bloc organized around negative unity and resistance to British taxation (1763-1774), and a second phase marked by the institutionalization of the hegemonic bloc through the Continental Congress, provincial conventions, and committees of safety (1774-1776). The analysis highlights the central role of institutional mediation, the relative autonomy of political and ideological processes, and the strategic sacrifice of short-term economic interests by leading classes in order to sustain bloc cohesion. By demonstrating how hegemony can be constructed and exercised in the absence of a consolidated state, the article contributes to historical sociology and offers a theoretically grounded reinterpretation of the American Revolution as a case of pre-state hegemonic formation.

articles.title: Consumer Protection Governance in Gendered Markets: Appearance Pressure, Consumer Awareness, and Gender-Differentiated Pricing in the Chandigarh–Mohali–Panchkula Tricity, India

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Gender-differentiated pricing, commonly termed the "Pink Tax," describes situations in which comparable products or services are priced differently by gender. While prior research has documented such price differences, less is known about the behavioral mechanisms shaping how consumers experience them. Drawing on the Political Economy of Beauty and consumer protection governance frameworks, this study examines how appearance pressure, gendered consumption behavior, and consumer awareness and price comparison behavior relate to experienced gender-differentiated pricing among 151 consumers surveyed in the Chandigarh–Mohali–Panchkula tricity, India. Using exploratory factor analysis, correlation, and multiple regression, the results indicate that appearance pressure (β = .407, p < .001) and consumer awareness and price comparison behavior (β = .320, p < .001) significantly predicted experienced gender-differentiated pricing, while gendered consumption behavior did not (β = .128, p = .120), together explaining 44.6% of the variance. These findings suggest that consumers' experiences of differential pricing are shaped more by social expectations around appearance and price awareness than by purchasing behavior alone. Robustness checks (Harman's single-factor test, variance inflation factors, and bootstrapped confidence intervals) support the stability of these results. Given the study's convenience sample and cross-sectional design, findings are presented as exploratory rather than generalizable, with implications framed as hypotheses for future regulatory attention rather than settled policy prescriptions. The study contributes an interdisciplinary behavioral perspective to consumer protection governance research in the Indian context.

articles.title: Evaluating the Youth Outcomes and Change Pathways of “Walk With Me”, a Peer Support Programme for Youths With or at Risk of Non-Suicidal Self-Injury in Singapore
articles.authors: Lyon Koh, Gerard Chung, Elizabeth Yee Min Chia, Anusha Agarwal, Sophie Cheng
articles.abstract: Introduction: Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) is common among youth and often serves social functions, yet most young people avoid formal services and turn to peers first. Walk With Me (WWM), a journey-based peer support programme in Singapore, pairs trained volunteers with youths who have or are at risk of NSSI. This study evaluated youth outcomes. Methods: Using a mixed-method, single-group, pre–post design, 36 youths (aged 15–25; 72% female) completed surveys before and after the programme. Eight outcomes spanning interpersonal and emotion-regulation domains were assessed, four theory-of-change pathways were tested and open-ended responses were analysed qualitatively. Results: All outcomes improved significantly from pre- to post-test, with medium to large effects; the largest gains were in emotion regulation and coping, and younger participants showed greater resilience gains. The four hypothesised change pathways were supported or partially supported; notably, encouragement to reach out predicted increased support-seeking. Youths rated their peer-supporter relationship highly, and qualitative accounts echoed these gains. Conclusion: WWM is linked to meaningful improvements in youths' social skills, support-seeking, communication, and emotion regulation, appearing to operate through a gradual peer relationship. As one of the first studies to test these mechanisms, it offers a promising foundation for rigorous evaluation.

articles.title: Dynamics of Skill Mismatch in the Workplace: Longitudinal Evidence from a Medium-Sized Japanese Company
articles.abstract: Although skill mismatch in the labor market is an important topic of discussion and research worldwide, that phenomenon in the Japanese labor market or organizations remains to be fully elucidated, despite the fact that Japan has a distinctive employment system. Therefore, using newly available data, such as longitudinal personnel data and employee satisfaction survey data, this study investigates the existence and determinants of vertical skill mismatch in a typical medium-sized Japanese company in order to address the dearth of similar literature in Japan. As a result, this study shows the vertical skill mismatch of frequent occurrence. Additionally, empirical results reveal: 1) job autonomy decreases the likelihood of vertical skill mismatch; 2) supervisors’ precise advice related to business activities for their subordinates reduces the likelihood of vertical skill mismatch; and 3) communication among employees in the workplace increases accessibility to skill matched roles. Career development in the Japanese company may not reflect a linear progression from easy work to more difficult work, but may rather be more of a mixed change involving under- and over-skilled mismatching.

articles.title: Lessons from Tanzania’s Ujamaa for Smart Settlements in Nepal: Social Justice and Economic Development

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: This article examines lessons Nepal can draw from Tanzania’s experience with Ujamaa, the African socialist development model initiated by President Nyerere in 1967. Using comparative policy analysis, published research, official documents, and exploratory field observations from selected Tanzanian locations, including the capital and villages in the Iringa Region, the study evaluates Ujamaa’s achievements and limitations. It assesses their relevance for Nepal’s landless populations and smart-settlement initiatives. The analysis focuses primarily on rural and peri-urban development and does not examine urban squatter housing and rural-to-urban migration. The comparison demonstrates that some lessons from Tanzania can be considered for Nepal’s own program. Ujamaa contributed to national integration, a shared linguistic identity, literacy, primary education, and rural services. However, it also reduced household autonomy, disrupted existing livelihood systems, and failed to achieve sustained agricultural productivity, employment generation, and income growth. The article also briefly discusses Nepal’s own Go to the Village Campaign of 1967, which had mixed success, and Korea’s generally successful 1970 Saemaul Undong movement for a comparative perspective of village-oriented national programs. The article proposes a Smart Settlement Framework for Nepal based on verified beneficiary identification, differentiated tenure and housing options, voluntary participation, livelihood-oriented site selection, serviced land, cooperative enterprise, accountable local governance, and measurable pathways from social protection to economic mobility.

articles.title: A New Prescription, Not a New Frame: Single Religious Belonging in Taiwan
articles.abstract: Social surveys commonly measure single religious belonging (SRB). Critics suggest SRB fails to group religionists meaningfully outside the West, where hybrid religiosity is normal. This study challenges that premise. Using the 2023 Taiwan Social Change Survey, I find SRB predicts 25 of 27 religiosity outcomes. Its power may vary. SRB separates Christians from everyone else almost perfectly, and Yiguandao just as well. Protestants and Chinese traditions rarely cross the Jesus worshipping boundary. And while Buddhists, Daoists and folk religionists share one pantheon, they rank it differently and follow different rules on diet, pilgrimage and initiation, so plural worship may mark syncretism rather than plural belonging. I then test whether granularity of SRB matters. Asking more denomination and taking refuge questions moves Buddhists and folk religionists between categories, but does not change the predicted pattern. Where SRB is thin, the remedy is a finer question about practice, not more boxes.

articles.title: Family Systems Intelligence in Neurodevelopmental Disability Care: A Conceptual Framework for Family-Centered Service
articles.abstract: Systems intelligence (Doherty, 2024; Doherty et al., 2026) offers a pathway for understanding how people perceive and act within complex interconnected systems. This article applies that concept to neurodevelopmental disability (NDD) service systems, where families and professionals coordinate care across clinical, educational, disability, and community contexts. We propose six components of family-centered interventions that build systems intelligence: systemic perception and self-positioning, shared interpretation, role negotiation, coordinated action, feedback responsiveness, and transferable capability. Three examples of family-centered approaches illustrate complementary pathways for developing systems intelligence across family, professional, and service-system relationships. The framework describes systems intelligence as a shared family-service capacity and identifies practical directions for research, training, service design, and equity.

articles.title: The Illiberal Academy: Typologies of Illiberal Institutions of Higher Learning
articles.abstract: As political illiberalism becomes a more prominent feature of contemporary democratic and hybrid political systems, the consequences that these emerging political forces have for institutions of higher education are only beginning to be explored. Universities occupy a central position in the ideological struggle for cultural hegemony: they produce knowledge, train elites, socialize large numbers of students, and shape the discursive environment. Illiberal movements recognize this and in addition to restricting the academic freedoms of university systems at large, also use these institutions as metapolitical instruments for achieving hegemony in both liberal democratic and authoritarian settings. Existing research offers little in terms of systematic frameworks for understanding the diversity of these organizations, which tend to be analyzed using case studies. This article addresses this gap by comparing illiberal universities across the US, EU and Russia and classifies them into four ideal types based on two primary factors: their origins and their funding sources which, we argue, influence the functions, incentive structures, and relations to political power for these universities. According to these two primary factors, we show that each ideal type operates according to a specific organizational logic. These findings demonstrate cross-national evidence for the multifaceted way in which illiberal movements engage with universities in the “third wave of autocratization.”

articles.title: Climate Action At Any Cost? Environmental Concern, Economic Trade-offs, and Regime Preferences
articles.abstract: Climate change confronts democratic governments with a difficult tension between effective climate action, economic prosperity, and democracy. But does this political trilemma also appear in citizens’ regime preferences? This paper examines how perceived climate threat and willingness to prioritize environmental protection over economic growth relate with support for democracy, technocracy, autocracy, and military rule. Using original comparative survey data collected in 2025 across eight European countries, I identify five profiles of regime preferences through cluster analysis and use multinomial regressions to examine how climate attitudes relate to profile membership. I find that low willingness to prioritize environmental protection over economic growth is associated with greater openness to autocratic forms of rule, including military rule, and that this association becomes substantially stronger as perceived climate threat increases. By contrast, when high climate threat is accompanied by high willingness to prioritize environmental protection even at the expense of economic growth, technocratic orientations prevail. These findings suggest that the institutional climate-growth-democracy trilemma may indeed have an individual-level counterpart: climate urgency is associated with different regime-preference profiles depending on citizens’ willingness to trade economic growth for environmental protection.

articles.title: The state of the research on parents with disabilities' involvement in the child protection system: A comprehensive review
articles.abstract: Background: This article provides a comprehensive overview of the global peer-reviewed research literature on the involvement of parents with disabilities in child protection. Materials: Using a systematic scoping review methodology that initially retrieved 10,471 articles, we identified 135 peer-reviewed articles. We charted the articles based on publication year, location of study, discipline, type of parental disability, methods, aspect of child protection studies, and whose voice was centered in the study. Results: We found a sharp global and cross-disciplinary increase in articles on this topic since 2010, with studies conducted in 17 countries and published in journals related to disability, child welfare, social work, mental health, and health. The majority focus on parents with intellectual and developmental disabilities or mental health disabilities. The most common areas of inquiry were the prevalence of child protection involvement and out-of-home care. Less common were articles about child protection processes, such as reporting, assessment, substantiation, services, case disposition, court processes, recurrence, and intervention. Most of the data used in the studies came from the professionals’ perspectives. Conclusion: Our study highlights significant gaps in the research and underscores the need for new directions in this field.

articles.title: From Business Accounting to Market Valuations
articles.abstract: In this study, we examine how accounting variables represent the core elements of firm activity and how the relations among these variables connect business accounting to market valuation. Building on this account, we develop a unified framework that expresses market values in accounting terms. A key contribution of this framework is that it places market-based and book-based measures of return within a single coherent structure. This unification, in turn, provides a new theoretical basis for refining central principles in corporate finance and valuation.

articles.title: Exact Linear Present Value
articles.abstract: In this study, we propose an exact, level-based counterpart to the widely used loglinear present value framework. This level-based framework preserves the core economic content of the loglinear approach while eliminating the need for approximation. The framework, however, goes beyond exactness. It also allows a richer analysis of price dynamics. Price changes are separated into anticipated movements and expectation revisions, and each component is further decomposed into cash-flow and discount-rate contributions. We apply the framework empirically to characterize aggregate stock price movements.

articles.title: Changing Relationship and Marriage Beliefs Across Partnership Formation Transitions in Germany
articles.abstract: This study explores changes in partnership and marriage beliefs across the life course in Germany. We conceptualize and empirically investigate relationship formation transitions as a mechanism for changing partnership and marriage beliefs, as they may reinforce or weaken cohort replacement effects. Adaptations in relationship beliefs may result either from increasing correspondence or unplanned contradictions of own relationship trajectories with “chrononormative” ideals around the standardized life cycle. We use fixed-effects panel data models based on the German pairfam data (2008-2022, N=11,705 respondents) to study how individuals’ partnership and marriage beliefs change across relationship formation transitions. Across LAT-entry and entry into cohabitation, beliefs in emotional benefits of partnerships increase, while beliefs in restrictions and stress decrease. Beliefs in financial benefits of partnerships increase when individuals enter cohabitation or marriage. Already with entry into LAT-relationships and cohabitation, support for marriage as a lifelong union rises moderately. Across entry into marriage, approval of marriage increases further, while nonmarital alternatives are viewed more critically. These adaptations following entry into marriage are more pronounced in East than West Germany. Our findings point to a strong couple norm and only partial deinstitutionalization and widespread approval of marriage.

articles.title: Characterizing Canadian Out-of-district Political Donations from 2015 to 2024
articles.abstract: Federal political representation in Canada is geographical: one Member of Parliament (MP) represents one electoral district. Despite this representational structure, Canadians can legally donate to a host of political entities, regardless of proximity. Using a public dataset from Elections Canada’s Open Data on Contributions matched with census data from Statistics Canada, we characterize broad patterns in Canadian out-of-district donation from 2015 to 2024. We find that out-of-district donations form a persistent share of donor-sourced funding to both candidates and district associations, averaging 40% across time, election periods, and party lines. While relatively constant through time, the propensity for out-of-district donation varies substantially across districts, beyond what spatial proximity alone would predict. Districts with higher population density, median household income, educational attainment, and visible minority proportions see higher rates of out-of-district giving, the same traits that predict donor prevalence generally in Canada. Despite its frequency, out-of-district donation in Canada remain largely regionalized; nearly half of donations that leave their district are received by a political entity in a neighbouring one, and few cross provincial lines. These and other findings provide a helpful characterization of this largely undocumented facet of Canadian political financing, and inform further research on effective representation in Canada and other nations with similar representational structures.

articles.title: Science through an artistic lens: scientific aesthetics and aesthetic exhibition practices with kinetic art installations in science museums
articles.authors: Na Zhang, Priscilla Van Even, Huang Yaping
articles.abstract: This chapter examines scientific aesthetics and the role of artistic mediation in contemporary science exhibitions, with a particular focus on kinetic art installations, a dynamic form of art that relies on movement and expressive motion. It situates aesthetic exhibition practices within the growing paradigm of experiential learning in science museums, which marks a shift from traditional top-down information transfer toward interactive exchange, as well as cognitive, sensorial, and aesthetic engagement of museum visitors through exhibition design. Rather than presenting science as static information to be passively absorbed, such exhibitions invite visitors to feel, reflect, and interpret through sensorial stimulation and meaningful cognitive engagement, reshaping how scientific knowledge is communicated, experienced, and understood. Drawing on the vision of the Exploratorium, a museum of science, art, and human perception founded by Frank Oppenheimer, the chapter approaches art and science as complementary modes of revealing and exploring natural phenomena. Through a series of case studies in science museums where kinetic art installations function as artistic mediation, the chapter explores how these artworks communicate scientific ideas through metaphor, movement, and interaction. These examples demonstrate how artistic mediation can render complex processes tangible and participatory. Together, they show how aesthetic exhibition practices foster active meaning-making and position science as a dynamic, interpretative process.

articles.title: The Politics of Crime Prevention: Evidence from Colombia

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Why do governments prevent crime in some places while neglecting others? Crime prevention policies are often viewed as too slow, diffuse, and politically intangible to generate electoral rewards. When implemented, existing research suggests they primarily serve to reward co-partisans or mobilize ideologically aligned voters. This article challenges that view by arguing that incumbents allocate crime-prevention resources to electorally competitive municipalities because these investments yield electoral returns. Using detailed project-level data from Colombia, I show that national incumbents disproportionately direct crime-prevention funds to municipalities where recent presidential elections were closely contested, rather than to areas with higher crime rates or strong partisan loyalties. I then demonstrate that these allocations increase the vote share of the right-wing incumbent coalition in subsequent elections. Drawing on quantitative analyses and interviews with policymakers and bureaucrats, I argue that these effects operate primarily through the visibility and attribution of crime prevention projects, particularly those aligned with right-wing issue ownership of public security.

articles.title: Scrolling the Nation: Banal Digital Nationalism on Short-Form Video Feeds
articles.abstract: This study inquired into the reproduction of banal digital nationalism on the algorithmically curated short-form video feeds. Rather than emphasizing overt nationalist content, I explored how situated, everyday user–platform interactions reproduce banal forms of nationalist ideology. Through digital diaries and post-hoc semi-structured interviews with Romanian users the analysis was attentive at the entanglement of social, affective and technological structures which habitually reinforce the physical and symbolic borders inherent in nationhood. Algorithmic “re-personalization” and “spacetimemattering” through memes, ads and nostalgic content were identified as forms of routine national (re-)production and normalization on the feed, users becoming oriented towards the nation and their being part of it beyond specific ideational contents. By focusing on an underexplored Eastern European context, the study contributes to research on digital nationalism while demonstrating the utility of new materialist sensibilities for investigating banal digital nationalism.

articles.title: Stable Contexts Are Not Static Causes: A Latent Variable Approach to Time-Varying Consequences of Stable Unobserved Heterogeneity
articles.abstract: Urban-health studies increasingly examine environmental co-occurrences, but longitudinal analyses often rely on fixed-effects (FE) models whose assumptions about stable unobserved heterogeneity are left implicit. This article uses a structural equation modeling (SEM) representation of FE to clarify a narrow but important point: stable, time-invariant, unobserved heterogeneity is controlled by conventional FE only when its contribution to repeated outcomes is also constant across waves. When stable histories of segregation, infrastructure, or governance have changing consequences as environmental co-occurrence configurations are reorganized, conventional FE models may leave residual confounding. I review the classical fixed-effects structural equation modeling (FE-SEM) representation, then present two diagnostic extensions: time-varying-loading FE-SEM (TVL-FE-SEM), a single-latent-dimension model with wave-specific loadings, and constant-and-deviation-loading FE-SEM (CDL-FE-SEM), a two-latent-dimension model that adapts the intercept/slope logic of latent growth modeling to separate common and deviation-loading profiles. A compact Monte Carlo simulation shows that classical FE-SEM recovers the true effect only when stable unobserved heterogeneity enters repeated outcomes with constant loadings, TVL-FE-SEM performs well when the same single latent source has changing loadings, and CDL-FE-SEM helps diagnose whether stable heterogeneity operates through more than one loading profile under a fixed-effects specification, though with finite-sample instability. An empirical illustration using Korean community-health data from 2021–2024 demonstrates the sequence as a diagnostic workflow.

articles.title: Dealing with Factor Mismeasurement
articles.abstract: Empirical implementation of asset pricing models faces a fundamental constraint. The true pricing factors implied by theory are unobservable, so researchers must rely on observable empirical factors. Because these factors are only proxies, they may contain measurement errors that distort estimated factor exposures, risk premia, and assessments of model performance. This study examines factor measurement errors and develops a methodology for assessing their empirical consequences. The methodology allows researchers to evaluate the reliability of asset pricing tests more carefully and draw more credible conclusions from empirical evidence.

articles.title: Shifting toward a Micro ICAPM
articles.abstract: Intertemporal asset pricing models typically begin with the market factor and introduce additional state variables to capture changes in investment opportunities over time. Empirically, these state variables have traditionally been proxied by macroeconomic variables because they reflect broad shifts in economic conditions affecting the aggregate opportunity set. These proxies are useful at the aggregate level, but less suited to representing variation in investment opportunities across individual assets. This study therefore develops a micro-level approach that replaces macroeconomic proxies with asset-specific variables. The central idea is that a broad set of such variables can more fully represent individual, time-varying investment opportunities.

articles.title: Out of the APT Shadow
articles.abstract: In empirical asset pricing, researchers often evaluate a pricing theory through its empirical factor model. This practice is widespread, but rests on a strong premise: the factor model must be a valid empirical proxy for the theory it claims to implement. In most applications, this premise is assumed rather than verified. Good performance alone is not decisive, because a factor model may reflect equilibrium pricing, arbitrage pricing, or both. This study addresses this ambiguity by separating risks arising solely from arbitrage considerations from those relevant to equilibrium pricing. It then tests whether a factor model truly represents equilibrium pricing theory.

articles.title: Operationalizing Qualitative Multimedia Content Analysis for Short-Form Video: A Methods and Data Study of Grooming Precursors Masked as Relationship Advice

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Objective: This methods and data article operationalizes qualitative multimedia content analysis (QMCA) for short-form video posts on TikTok and Instagram Reels, focusing on the method's execution and the frequency structure of observable grooming-precursor cues masked as relationship advice. Method: A purposive corpus of 100 public short-form videos, evenly split between TikTok and Instagram, was archived, de-identified, and coded using MAXQDA 24 for time-segment coding and Excel for the codebook, audit trail, and thresholds. A five-pass routine separated visual features, audio features, on-screen text, and relational/boundary cues. Category development relied on same-document co-occurrence, with recurrence requiring five or more distinct posts. Results: The final codebook contained 289 codes and produced 1,233 post-level feature hits. Recurrence concentrated in presentation-layer categories: Parasocial Proximity and Platform Normalization appeared in all 100 posts, and Intimate Setting Cues in 80. Covert precursor categories recurred less often: Power Imbalance Normalization in 30 posts, Coercive Reframing in 15, Boundary Erosion in 14, and Isolation and Secrecy in 10. Conclusions: QMCA provides an auditable method for documenting how short-form advice content packages relational scripts through camera, voice, setting, captioning, and platform conventions. The taxonomy supports prevention-oriented screening without inferring creator intent or labeling any post as grooming.

articles.title: The missing quadrant: perceived voluntariness, option sets and the acceptance of green digital tools
articles.authors: Maha Jehanzeb, Talha Murtaza, Rida Safdar
articles.abstract: Technology acceptance research measures voluntariness as a perception and, in its consumer flagship, assumes it outright, while parallel stream studies explicitly mandate use. It is between the perception and the mandate that a state lies which neither can classify: a use that is formally optional and reported as chosen while the adopter’s set of viable alternatives has been closed off by conditions beyond their control. This paper names that state foreclosed adoption, where the voluntariness assumption of acceptance research is adapted through the lens of the self-determination theory, whose definition of autonomy as endorsement rather than independence entails that the experience of free adoption cannot certify that alternatives existed. The paper goes on to develop a typology of adoption states (volitional, foreclosed, mandated), three foreclosure mechanisms (economic, architectural, relational) with distinct sources and visibilities, an account of leadership style as the mechanism converting foreclosure into internalisation or bare compliance, and eight propositions with an operationalisation agenda. Green digital technology is argued to be the domain where the resulting misclassification costs most, because foreclosed green adoptions are counted twice over, as voluntary and as value driven, inflating estimates of environmental motivation in research and in organisational sustainability metrics.

articles.title: Humanity after the peak: long-run population and human-capital pathways for global environmental change
articles.abstract: Population and human-capital pathways are central to global environmental change research, yet most widely used demographic projections end in 2100. This creates a time-horizon problem for slow-moving environmental processes, including sea-level rise, land-use change, long-lived infrastructure, food-system transformation and adaptation across generations. We extend Shared Socioeconomic Pathways population and human-capital scenarios to 2300 and examine how peak population gives way to long-run demographic decline, aging and regional redistribution. In the middle-of-the-road pathway, the global population declines to about 4.2 billion by 2300. In the sustainability pathway, it approaches 1 billion. These are not extinction scenarios, but they describe a profound change in the social and demographic setting in which environmental demand, exposure, adaptation and policy operate. The results show that the post-2100 period cannot be treated as a simple continuation of twentieth-century population growth. A smaller, older and more educated world may reduce some overall pressures while intensifying others, especially around labor, care, migration and uneven regional change. Long-run environmental analysis, therefore, needs population pathways that extend beyond 2100 and include not only population size, but also age, education, spatial distribution and demographic momentum.

articles.title: Social spending and democratic institutions in Southeast Asia: A comparative study between Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and the Philippines
articles.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to analyse how democratic institutions affects social spending formations in the context of developing countries. Furthermore, this essay will also challenge the theory that the government system (majoritarian versus consensus democracy) influences the magnitude of social spending and welfare commitment, especially in Southeast Asian democracies, namely, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and the Philippines. Design/methodology/approach This research uses descriptive statistics and qualitative data to match social spending with the development of democratisation in four cases. Findings The main argument is whether the presence of democratic institutions encourages the government to be more open, citizen-oriented and responsive or whether the inclusive political conditions will create more open public participation in the policymaking process.
