Thus, in the context of developing countries, public participation will be more likely to demand social policies. Research limitations/implications It has not been able to undertake a more detailed impact evaluation assessment of the development and change of democratic institutions towards policy outcomes within a shorter temporal scope. In addition, this thesis does not also provide details or explanations about the interaction process between particular democratic institutions and specific social policy sectors. Practical implications The process of interactions between particular electoral systems. For instance, the contribution to the emergence of policy in the health services sector or conducting research in normative democratic institutions such as public awareness of the importance of public participation in shaping and directing the implementation of poverty reduction policies could be studied, by using the historical institutionalism approach. Originality/value The impact of certain political institutions on public policy has become a very important discussion in the new institutionalism perspective. Social policy (social spending) as a manifestation of government’s commitment towards welfare is the result of institutional arrangement. In the context of developing countries, where social policy is needed to fulfill the basic needs of citizens, it is important to identify what kind of institutional formations are conducive to the development of social policy. This essay will analyse how democratic institutions affects social spending formations in the context of developing countries.

articles.title: A Rejoinder to 'Still Instrumentally Inclusive' (Turnbull-Dugarte & López Ortega)
articles.abstract: Turnbull-Dugarte and López Ortega's "Still Instrumentally Inclusive" (the Response) answers my replication (the Comment) of their 2024 American Political Science Review paper (the Article) with, among other things, a multiverse of 2,970 analyses based on eighteen different weighting schemes, randomization inference, and a trichotomous moderator. As I show in this rejoinder, each is undermined by bona fide errors in their code, their writing, and their interpretation. First, the multiverse is just many correlated variants of the same test. This is in large part due to the weighting schemes which suffer multiple problems (some due to code errors, some intrinsic), and are largely correlated variations on one weighting scheme. Second, due to code errors the randomization inference compares a weighted statistic against an unweighted null and, in the two heterogeneity tests, permutes the interaction column rather than treatment assignment column. Every permutation p-value the Response reports is therefore computed against the wrong reference distribution; when they are recomputed correctly, two of the five it reports as significant are no longer so, and they are the two the Response emphasizes. Third, the trichotomous moderator is erroneously described as terciles, but it is in fact based on non-tercile cutpoints. The key subgroup effect reported in the Response thus rests on comparing just thirty high-weight control respondents against thirty-one high-weight treated respondents, and ends up reaffirming my original point that the heterogeneity in study 2 is with respect to weights, and not immigration sentiment as their theory predicts. I close by documenting seven claims in the Response that are untrue or misleading.

articles.title: Designing engagement: A Research through Design approach to cultivating relational motivation for community-supported agriculture
articles.authors: Sota Takagi, Maoko Fujisaki, Mitsuyo Toyoda, Takumi Ohashi
articles.abstract: Global challenges such as climate change and food insecurity are closely linked to the unsustainable structures of dominant food systems. These systems are reinforced by entrenched mental models that treat consumers as passive buyers and agriculture as mere market transaction. Community-Supported Agriculture (CSA) offers a locally grounded model in which producers and consumers share the risks and benefits of production, holding potential to challenge these structures and foster new relationships and behaviors that contribute to systemic food system change. However, CSA remains underdeveloped in Japan, and how participation motivations are relationally generated through design remains poorly understood. This study examines how design interventions can cultivate relational motivation: forms of engagement arising through social connection and shared values rather than individual preference alone. A Research through Design (RtD) approach was employed to examine a collaborative design intervention in Isumi, Chiba, Japan (October 2025). It followed five phases: (1) educational sessions on CSA and natural farming, (2) a chef-curated meal featuring locally grown produce, (3) a farm field tour, (4) a facilitated Philosophy for Children (p4c) dialogue, and (5) a co-creation workshop. Eleven participants attended, supported by eight collaborators including a producer, a chef, local staff, and researchers. Pre- and post-intervention questionnaires (seven-point Likert scales) and thematic analysis of dialogue and workshop data were used for analysis. Quantitative analysis (Wilcoxon signed-rank test) showed a significant increase in participants’ ethical food-selection intention (p = .046, r = .63), and eight of ten reported increased willingness to join CSA despite half having had no prior awareness. Thematic analysis identified three themes: deepened understanding of natural farming, intergenerational responsibility for food culture, and critical reflection on production structures. These themes were translated into concrete CSA visions in the co-creation workshop. Through RtD, the study derived design principles for an entry-point intervention to cultivate participation intentions toward CSA: (1) sequential integration of learning, experience, and reflection; (2) cross-domain intermediary collaboration as social infrastructure; and (3) embodied and relational ethics that translate abstract values into situated action. These principles offer actionable guidance for designers, educators, and policymakers seeking to lower barriers to CSA participation within local communities.

articles.title: Cheap Labor, Expensive Consequences: Determinants Behind Persisting Exploitative Labor Practices in India's Labor Market
articles.abstract: India’s recent economic trajectory has been marked by a striking paradox. Periods of high aggregate growth, expanding urbanization, and integration into domestic and global value chains have coexisted with mass labor informality, insecure employment, weak bargaining power, and uneven access to legal protection. This paper examines whether India’s economic growth has substantially been dependent on exploitative labor, understood not merely as low pay, but as a labor regime characterized by precarity, restricted worker voice, externalization of social costs, and structurally unequal exposure to risk, while recognizing the link between labor exploitation and the architecture of growth rather than treating it solely as a distributive or moral problem. The paper recommends further policy to prevent exploitative labor practices for socio-economic development, calling for the inclusion in development planning to promote cultural identity, economic resilience, diversity, and community participation as a structural support in multiple sectors through responsible governance and business practices.

articles.title: Combining survey questions with a Bayesian bootstrap method improves election forecasts
articles.authors: Henrik Olsson, Wandi Bruine de Bruin, Mirta Galesic, Drazen Prelec

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: We present a Bayesian bootstrap method for election forecasting that integrates traditional own-intention questions with wisdom-of-crowds questions, which ask for social-circle expectations and election forecasts. Across the 2018, 2020, and 2024 U.S. elections, wisdom-of-crowds questions consistently outperformed own-intention questions in predicting vote shares. The Bayesian bootstrap combines these questions in a theoretically justified way, assigning weights based on their inferred informational value. The main assumption is that election winner expectations for a given participant are themselves an optimal Bayesian forecast in light of all evidence available to that participant. Social-circle expectations contribute the most to the Bayesian bootstrap forecast, as they reduce demographic biases and capture hidden voter preferences. The method improves forecast accuracy across diverse electoral contexts, offering a principled approach to combining polling questions and suggesting applicability to forecasting other social phenomena.

articles.title: Directing internal attention during sentence reading
articles.authors: Rhianna Lowri Watt, Sage Boettcher, Anna C Nobre, Kate Nation, Dejan Draschkow, Blaine Butler
articles.abstract: Selective attention plays a central role in identifying and prioritising relevant memories (internal attention), but internal attention’s involvement in selecting relevant content for language comprehension is not understood. In two preregistered experiments, we tested the utility of anaphoric expressions as retrodictive cues to guide content selection. Participants read sentences, followed by anaphoric expressions (retrocues) that referred back to one of two target words contained in the sentence. Subsequently, participants were prompted to identify which target word had been referred to. We manipulated the predictability of the anaphoric expression across experiments (Experiment 1: predictive; Experiment 2: non-predictive). We show improved response performance for cued words, even when the retrocue was non-predictive. This parallels classic patterns of automatic attentional selection of memory contents in visual working memory. Our findings suggest that anaphoric devices act through internal attention to select language content maintained in memory to serve ongoing comprehension.

articles.title: Title: Sport for Preventing Violent Extremism: A Systematic Scoping Review
articles.abstract: Background: Violent Extremism is a global threat, prompting both the United Nations and its member states to prioritize prevention efforts. The growth of Violent Extremism prevention through sport or sport-based interventions has been reported in several scholarly studies and en dorsed by the United Nations. These studies have also reported a shift in efforts to prevent future forms of Violent Extremism towards targeting potential future violent extremists and preventing radicalization through Sport programs. Though, there is a lack of knowledge regarding the poten tial mechanisms, methods and approaches for preventing Violent Extremism (PVE) through SDP. This study aims to explore the best practices for using SDP/Sport as a tool in PVE. Methods: A systematic scoping review was conducted by using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) template by (Tricco et al., 2018) on five databases (i.e., Scopus, SportDiscus, Scielo, Sociological ABS, SocIndex) between 2000 and February 2025. A total of 1,284 records were identified and were narrowed to 12 references for full extraction. Results: The review found that SDP/sport and PVE research gained momentum after 2019, with publications focusing on countering and preventing violent extremism, resilience building, and youth deradicalization, aligning with Sustainable Development Goals 3, 10, and 16. Six of the included studies were empirical, five were literature reviews, and one was a personal experience of the researcher. Empirical studies were conducted in Russia, Australia, India, Tajikistan, Jordan, Europe, Nigeria, Kenya and Uganda. Therefore, peace education curricula were implemented in Nigeria, India, Tajikistan and Jordan, though girls/women were notably absent as beneficiaries. The findings emphasize the need for updated methodologies and inclusive approaches to enhance intervention effectiveness. Conclusion: This review demonstrates that sport can play a powerful role in preventing violent extremism by fostering youth resilience and community belonging. Conversely, current research lacks consistency, clear frameworks, and meaningful inclusion of local voices. To advance the field, future studies should broaden the scope of PVE to include related concepts, such as crime and violence prevention, and draw on grey literature to build a more comprehensive and grounded understanding.

articles.title: When the Well-Off Feel Left Behind: Income Misperception and Populist Attitudes
articles.authors: Thilo N.H. Albers, Daniel Bischof, Felix Kersting, Fabian Kosse
articles.abstract: Why do materially secure citizens embrace populist attitudes? Research on the populist right has focused primarily on economically vulnerable voters and left-behind places, leaving unclear why support extends to citizens who are objectively well off. We argue that a belief-based source of grievance helps explain this puzzle: citizens may underestimate their relative economic standing and feel deprived despite material security. Using a survey module embedded in the Innovation Sample of the German Socio-Economic Panel, we show that pessimistic income-rank misperceptions predict stronger populist attitudes conditional on actual rank. Instrumental-variable and within-household analyses strengthen a causal interpretation. A preregistered survey experiment randomly provides personalized information about respondents' actual income percentile. The control arm replicates the observational pattern; the treatment corrects beliefs and shifts income satisfaction, but does not reduce populist attitudes. Economic grievance can therefore travel upward through perceived status, while becoming politically resistant once organized by populist narratives.

articles.title: What Is Coercion?
articles.abstract: A brief monograph investigating the subject of coercion, comparing the perspectives of Sarah Conly's "Seduction, Rape, and Coercion", Patrick Bratton's "When Is Coercion Successful?: And Why Can’t We Agree on It?", and H.J. McCloskey's "Coercion: Its Nature and Significance". It is concluded that coercion is separate from persuasion by its method of action in that coercion threatens identity and persuasion does not. There is also a distinction between legitimate and illegitimate coercion.

articles.title: Tool or Trend? Workload, Confidence, and the Conditions for Generative AI Adoption in Research Administration
articles.abstract: Generative AI is rapidly transforming white-collar work; however, little is known about its uptake in research administration, a specialized field of non-routine, judgement-dependent labour. This study reports the findings from a cross-sectional survey of researchers and research administrative staff at a large academic research hospital in Toronto, Canada (n = 119). Almost three-quarters of respondents (73%) reported using generative AI tools for research administrative work. Four outcome variables, Frequency, Effectiveness, Impact, and Quality of generative AI use, were strongly intercorrelated, indicating that respondents who used the tools more frequently also rated them more favourably across all three evaluative dimensions. Self-assessed confidence positively predicted evaluations of the tools, whereas job security concern was negatively associated with evaluations of generative AI. Respondents who iteratively refined outputs rated the tools more favourably than those who abandoned their attempts at using them, while heavier workloads were associated with less favourable quality perceptions. These findings suggest that realizing generative AI’s potential in administrative work depends on the user’s skills, confidence, and working conditions, rather than the tools themselves.

articles.title: Is the Future Modular? Mapping Preferences, Benefits, and Risks of Modular Journalism across three Audience Segments
articles.authors: Sophie Morosoli, Hannes Cools, Natali Helberger
articles.abstract: One of the ways in which GenAI could change the future of news is modular journalism (MJ) – presenting news in novel, more fluid, personalized and interactive formats that respond and adjust to the individual preferences of users. Being more responsive to users' individual needs through AI-supported forms of personalization could unlock new ways of catering to diverse or underserved audiences, and potentially even reduce news avoidance and information overload or serve as the foundation for new news experiences. This study investigates audience evaluations and willingness to pay for MJ through focus groups (N=26) with three diverse user segments: basic subscribers, adolescents, and individuals with migration backgrounds. Findings reveal that particularly young adults and individuals with migration backgrounds are interested in MJ, valuing flexibility and engagement, though concerns exist about oversimplification of serious topics. Participants favor personalization with user agency over algorithmic curation to preserve content diversity. Willingness to pay is mixed; MJ alone has limited appeal but adds value when integrated into existing subscriptions. Young adults are most willing to pay, especially with trial access. These findings illustrate that there is a potential for MJ to engage audiences with customizable formats, user-controlled personalization, and editorial integrity, and in doing so enhance accessibility, and potentially reduce news avoidance.

articles.title: Recursive Requisite Variety: A Cross-Level Theory of Regulatory Capacity and Control Loss
articles.abstract: Control is lost in structurally similar ways across systems that share no subject matter: an individual who can no longer check what a machine produced, a building whose automation degrades along the dimension it does not sense, a project organization that adds reviewers without adding scrutiny, and a workforce that delegates judgment to a system it cannot audit. These failures are ordinarily explained by four unconnected literatures. This article argues that they instantiate a common mechanism, and it offers that mechanism as a theoretical proposal rather than a tested account. Regulatory capacity is finite and must be allocated across scale, time, and dimension. Delegation does not remove regulatory load; it converts execution load into verification load, while the capability that discharges verification load is maintained largely as a by-product of execution and therefore decays under delegation. Because the allocation decision draws on the same bounded budget, the locally rational response to overload increases the load that produced it, and recovery requires a capacity injection exceeding the original deficit. The resulting structure is termed recursive requisite variety: the same allocation failure recurs at every level of a nested system, and a regulator’s effective variety is bounded by the effective rather than the nominal variety of the regulators beneath it. Seven falsifiable propositions are derived; none is tested here. The instantiations are conceptual recoveries with illustrative evidence rather than tests of the mechanism, and the article states at each level which of the two it is offering. Three of the propositions were not located, in the form stated here, in the scoping audit reported below: redundant regulators drawing on a shared source add effective variety only in proportion to their independent failure share; artefacts carrying neither recoverable provenance nor an independently checkable criterion impose verification load that no capacity can discharge; and overload is characteristically not registered by the actor experiencing it, because the delegate’s output exhibits the surface properties of reliable feedback.

articles.title: Reliability-Aware Sexism Detection: Combining DPO with Annotator Agreement and Token-Level Confidence Scoring
articles.authors: Hadi Mohammadi, Shihan Wang, Masoume M. Raeissi, Anastasia Giachanou
articles.abstract: The detection of online sexism remains an open problem. Sexism detection is inherently subjective, yet most existing systems reduce multi-annotator labels to a single majority decision and treat all instances uniformly. This ignores two informative signals: annotator agreement and model uncertainty. We propose RA-DPO (Reliability-Aware Direct Preference Optimization), which integrates annotator agreement, model confidence, and a token-level uncertainty signal into a single reliability score. RA-DPO uses this score to select high-value preference pairs during training and to support inference-time abstention, which allows the model to trade coverage for accuracy. We evaluate RA-DPO on 6,920 multilingual posts from EXIST 2023, fine-tune OpenAI gpt-4o base via DPO, and validate on two open-weight 3B models (Llama, Qwen). Results show that training on the top 30% most reliable pairs matches full-data DPO which indicates that reliability-aware selection can reduce training cost without sacrificing performance. At inference, selective prediction reaches 96.2% accuracy at 50% coverage in the true-agreement setting and 88.7% in the deployable predicted-agreement setting, both exceeding the 85.3% no-agreement baseline. These results suggest that accounting for annotation uncertainty is beneficial for both efficient training and reliable deployment in subjective classification.

articles.title: Effects of Questionnaire Notifications on Engagement and Attrition in an Ecological Momentary Assessment Study: Longitudinal Observational Study
articles.authors: Daniel Dvořák, Martin Kreidl, Martin Tancoš
articles.abstract: Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) studies are widely used in mobile health (mHealth) research and interventions. EMA requires participants to repeatedly open short questionnaires announced by smartphone notifications, so notification scheduling is a central design decision. Yet evidence on how repeated prompts shape short-term engagement and long-term attrition remains fragmented. We examined (a) how notification order within a measurement window relates to the timing and likelihood of questionnaire opening, and (b) whether the number of notifications within a burst relates to permanent disengagement, in a 12-month, multi-burst smartphone EMA study of Czech adolescents. We analyzed paradata from the FUTURE project, an observational EMA study of 201 adolescents (13–17 years). Four 14-day bursts each contained up to four short questionnaires per day, with up to 10 notifications per questionnaire window. Time from first notification to opening was modeled with Cox survival models with respondent-level frailty. Permanent dropout was modeled with logistic regression at the person-burst level. We tested whether demographics, timing, and the momentary phone context (screen activity, app use) moderated the notification effects. Analyses used Stata 18. A total of 26,007 questionnaires were notified. Of these, 17,668 (67.9%) were opened. Within a measurement window, among questionnaires still unopened, later reminders were associated with a slightly higher chance of opening (hazard ratio [HR] 1.13, 95% CI 1.06–1.19; P<.001), and this estimate was stable across all models, and we found no sign of within-window reminder fatigue. Gender, age, and socioeconomic status changed this pattern only marginally. The phone context mattered more. When the screen was already on (interaction HR 0.862, 95% CI 0.846–0.878), or social media (HR 0.884, 95% CI 0.856–0.913) or messaging (HR 0.884, 95% CI 0.844–0.926) was in use (all P<.001), reminders were less efficient. Regarding study dropout, 86 of 201 participants (43%) disengaged permanently. More reminders within a burst were associated with slightly lower odds of study dropout (fully adjusted odds ratio [OR] 0.981, 95% CI 0.965–0.996; P=.01), a small association that was stable across all model specifications (OR 0.978–0.984). In this adolescent EMA study, engagement was front-loaded: most openings came soon after the first prompt, but even later notifications had a positive effect on questionnaire engagement. So, within each measurement window, more prompts are better. This holds across all socio-demographics. Repeated reminders showed no sign of backfiring on study dropout. In fact, more reminders went with slightly lower study dropout. Responsiveness depended on what the phone was doing just before the first prompt. Context-aware prompting (avoiding prompts especially if a social media or a messaging app are open) is a more efficient design lever than simply adding reminders.

articles.title: State and local attitudes toward household electrification in California: evidence from a large survey
articles.authors: Gabriel De Roche, Sophia Tomany de Brito, Yohan Min, Sanjay Poudel, Madalsa Singh, Patricia Hidalgo-Gonzalez, Ranjit Deshmukh, Grace C. Wu, Matto Mildenberger

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Decarbonizing residential energy depends on millions of households making millions of purchasing decisions across multiple household electrification technologies, especially solar and storage systems, electric vehicles, heat pumps, and induction stoves. This paper describes consumer attitudes towards household electrification using a large representative survey of 7,158 households in California, with data collected in Spring 2025 from a stratified sample that includes large subgroups across all of California's climate zones as well as from census tracts designated as Disadvantaged Communities by the state. Alongside a wide range of sociodemographic and attitudinal predictors of current adoption, we measure future adoption interest with a personalized contingent-valuation measure of the minimum financial incentive/subsidy required to adopt along a technology-specific subsidy ladder. Leveraging the large statewide sample size, we also use multilevel regression with post-stratification (MRP) to estimate future adoption rates for each of California's 9,129 census tracts for every threshold along this subsidy ladder. We find substantial latent demand, especially for technologies with low current adoption. We also find heterogeneity across technologies in consumers' sensitivity to subsidies and that attitudinal predictors (and especially beliefs about cost, health, and safety benefits) dominate sociodemographic predictors. These results have direct implications for active policy design. Information campaigns designed to shift beliefs about health and safety play an important complementary role alongside cost-focused messages. Our geographically fine-grained estimates of future adoption at the census tract level provide rich local data for policy-makers, researchers, and practitioners designing incentive programs and planning grid infrastructure as California households continue to electrify.

articles.title: What Does Frontier Access Buy? Benchmarking LLM Access Tiers and the Reproducibility Case for Open Weights in Survey Coding
articles.abstract: Social scientists coding open-ended survey responses with large language models (LLMs) face a tradeoff between proprietary frontier systems, cheaper commercial alternatives, and open-weight models that can be audited and self-hosted. This study benchmarks eighteen LLMs across four access tiers, from proprietary flagships to open-weight models small enough to run on a laptop, zero-shot against a human consensus on three open-ended questions from a probability-sampled U.S. panel. External validation adds a British Election Study task and an online-comment emotion task (GoEmotions), spanning five tasks in three contexts. The flagship proprietary models' average margin over their cheaper counterparts is statistically indistinguishable from zero, despite stronger general-benchmark performance. Pricing tells the same story: frontier models cost 1.3–6× more per token, yet for most of them some cheaper model is also more accurate, and the field's second-best macro F1 comes from its cheapest closed model. Open-weight models have largely caught up. The largest ones match both proprietary tiers on cell-level agreement, while on the stricter macro F1 they trail by about two points on average. They reach this at no per-call cost, with the reproducibility and data-privacy advantages of self-hosting. Both patterns hold out of domain. The leading models, closed and open alike, agree with a trained human coder about as well as the two coders agree with each other. Failure is patterned. Errors concentrate on interpretive categories where the human coders themselves disagreed, and on longer responses, penalties from which frontier prices buy little relief. The caveat is scale. Laptop-scale models show strong cell-level agreement but trail further on macro F1, so fully local deployment carries a modest, task-dependent accuracy cost. Hardware scale and question difficulty, not price or license, are the binding constraints on these tasks.

articles.title: Request routing services undermine the reproducibility of open weight LLMs
articles.authors: Joe Higton, Joshua A. Tucker, Christopher Barrie
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now a standard tool for classifying text in social science. To make these classifications reproducible, researchers are often advised to use open weight models and to set the sampling temperature to zero. We show that this advice is insufficient when models are accessed through a request-routing service, in which queries are sent to different hosting providers through a single API. Using a popular request-routing service, OpenRouter, we classify British manifesto sentences for ideology 100 times per sentence across eight models and 33 hosting providers, alongside five model configurations served on our own hardware, generating approximately 1m classification draws. When using the request-routing service, open weight models consistently fail to return deterministic outputs. Depending on the model, only 26% to 92% of sentences receive the same label in all repeated classifications. This variation is not solely due to different providers fielding queries: for five of the eight models, the majority of classification variance arises within providers. On our own hardware, the same task is perfectly reproducible at temperature=0. We conclude that reproducibility depends on the entire model hosting environment, and recommend that researchers report the fullest available metadata and raw responses when using LLMs.

articles.title: Same Facts, Different Meanings: Factual Information, Interpretation, and Attitude Change
articles.abstract: A key puzzle in the political information literature is why factual information reliably updates citizens’ beliefs about the fact in question but rarely shifts downstream political attitudes. Using two preregistered survey experiments (N ≈ 3,250) covering eleven issues across economic indicators and misstatements by prominent political figures, this paper makes two contributions. First, we test whether the muted effect of factual information on downstream attitudes holds for outcomes that are less entrenched and more proximate to the information than those tested in prior work—such as economic evaluations and perceptions of politicians’ honesty and competence—and find that even these outcomes respond only modestly. Second, we develop and empirically test a framework of six adjacent belief dimensions—regarding causes, relevance, and intent—through which factual information may be reinterpreted in ways that reshape its political meaning. We find evidence of adjacent belief updating, although concentrated on specific dimensions rather than widespread. The strongest finding is that individuals who learn that a favored politician made an inaccurate claim concede the inaccuracy but shift toward viewing the statement as figurative, with sizable effects across two independent studies. Importantly, where adjacent belief adjustment occurs, its direction is contingent on individuals’ predispositions. Uncongenial information triggers adjustment that attenuates the political implications of the fact, while congenial information triggers no such adjustment or small shifts in the opposite direction. Together, the results illustrate how parallel trends in factual accuracy can coexist with divergent trends in how those facts are politically interpreted.

articles.title: Measuring Perceptions of Extreme Weather Events and Climate Change
articles.authors: Clara Brügge, Patrick Kraft, Franziska Quoß
articles.abstract: As climate change increases the frequency and severity of extreme weather events (EWEs), people worldwide are beginning to experience these impacts firsthand. While a growing body of research has explored how this direct experience of EWEs affects public perceptions, attitudes, and behaviors, findings remain inconclusive. A central challenge in this literature is the large researcher degrees of freedom in operationalizing EWEs. This inconsistency partly stems from a lack of theoretical and empirical clarity regarding what the public actually perceives as an EWE. Previous work has shown a low correspondence between subjective perceptions and objective meteorological data, highlighting a disconnect between scientific definitions and the experience of laypeople. To address this gap, we investigate how average citizens conceptualize EWEs using a high-quality panel survey conducted in Switzerland. We field an open-ended survey question with experimental variation in its wording and use large language models (LLMs) to classify the content of responses across multiple dimensions – including the type of event, its regional focus, and its relation to climate change. Validating the classification against human coding and benchmarking it against fine-grained objective weather data, we find that respondents draw on a wide range of considerations, that question wording – especially a local cue – strongly shapes responses while explicit climate-change priming does not, and that open-ended responses correspond at least as closely to objective weather data as a targeted closed-ended item. We discuss the promise and limitations of LLM-based measurement for research on climate and extreme weather perceptions.

articles.title: Long-run political change after the Great Recession
articles.abstract: What are the long-run political consequences of economic crises? We study the Great Recession in the United States, exploiting geographic variation in unemployment shocks. Harder-hit counties shifted toward Democratic candidates. House gains persisted through 2022, after the shock's employment effects had dissipated, while presidential gains attenuated after 2016. House gains did not track local recovery or Republican incumbency, which weighs against simple retrospective voting accounts. Harder-hit places also showed no shift toward right-wing populist candidates or movements. Instead, survey and ballot measure evidence points to economic scarring and demand for protection: residents of harder-hit places remained pessimistic about their economic prospects, even as personal finances recovered, and became more supportive of social protection. Taken together, the findings suggest that a crisis can durably reshape what affected communities demand from government after acute local labor market distress has subsided.

articles.title: Social norms solve coordination problems paradoxically created by shared interests
articles.authors: Minhua Yan, Yuanmei Li, Zhizhong Li, Robert Boyd, Sarah Mathew
articles.abstract: Human cooperation is motivated both by shared interests arising from kinship and friendship and by social norms, but whether these mechanisms substitute for or complement one another remains debated. Cooperative farming among Derung horticulturalists offers an ideal study context, because most cofarming occurs among kin or friends, and a norm prescribes equal harvest division by household regardless of contributions. We show that this norm solves two problems that shared interests cannot solve, or may even exacerbate. First, shared interests expand the range of acceptable divisions, making coordination harder. By specifying a salient division, the norm resolves this problem. Second, cofarmers often misperceive how much their partner benefits. By prescribing a division independent of cost-benefit assessments, the norm prevents these differences from unraveling cooperation. The complementary action of norms and shared interests may explain why humans cooperate with kin and friends more than other animals.

articles.title: Poverty and Caregiver Mental Health are Related to Infant and Toddler Resting State Brain Networks: Insights from fNIRS
articles.authors: Kaja K. Jasińska, Hannah Whitehead, Sharon Wolf, Dr Fabrice Tanoh, Stephanie Bugden, Brooke Wortsman, Amy Ogan
articles.abstract: Significance: The first three years of life represent a period of heightened neural plasticity, during which early adversity—such as poverty and maternal stress—can shape long-term developmental trajectories. However, little is known about how these adversities are linked to neural network organization in infants and toddlers living in low-resource settings. Aim: This study examined how prenatal exposure to maternal poverty and mental health symptoms relates to neural network organization in early childhood. Approach: We conducted a longitudinal study with 42 children (6–36 months old) from economically-vulnerable households in rural Côte d’Ivoire. Maternal multidimensional poverty and mental health symptoms were assessed around conception and during pregnancy. Two years later, children’s development was measured using the Caregiver Reported Early Development Instruments (CREDI), and resting-state brain activity was recorded using portable functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Graph-theoretic metrics of functional connectivity, including segregation, integration, and small-worldness, were computed to characterize neural network organization. Results: Greater exposure to poverty was associated with reduced network segregation and integration. In contrast, higher maternal mental health symptoms were linked to increased segregation and integration. These findings suggest that deprivation and maternal stress differentially relate to early neural network architecture. Conclusions: Our results align with dimensional models of adversity, and suggest that deprivation (related to poverty) and threat/unpredictability (related to maternal mental health and caregiving) may become biologically embedded. These findings underscore the importance of addressing both structural poverty and maternal mental health during pregnancy and early childhood to promote healthy brain development in high-adversity contexts.

articles.title: Bayesian estimation in multiple comparisons
articles.abstract: Traditional regression models typically estimate parameters for a factor F by designating one level as a reference (intercept) and calculating slopes for other levels of F. While this approach often aligns with our research question(s), it limits direct comparisons between all pairs of levels within F and requires additional procedures for generating these comparisons. Moreover, Frequentist methods often rely on corrections (e.g., Bonferroni or Tukey), which can reduce statistical power and inflate uncertainty by mechanically widening confidence intervals. This paper demonstrates how Bayesian hierarchical models provide a robust framework for parameter estimation in the context of multiple comparisons. By leveraging entire posterior distributions, these models produce estimates for all pairwise comparisons without requiring post hoc adjustments. The hierarchical structure, combined with the use of priors, naturally incorporates shrinkage, pulling extreme estimates toward the overall mean. This regularization improves the stability and reliability of estimates, particularly in the presence of sparse or noisy data, and leads to more conservative comparisons. Bayesian models also offer a flexible framework for addressing heteroscedasticity by directly modeling variance structures and incorporating them into the posterior distribution. The result is a coherent approach to exploring differences between levels of F, where parameter estimates reflect the full uncertainty of the data.

articles.title: Who Pays for the Church? Religious Clientelism and Broker Compensation in Postwar Italy
articles.abstract: In many contexts, religious leaders mobilize support for allied politicians. These mobilization efforts are often assumed to be part of brokerage agreements in which politicians provide material compensation once elected. Despite how common these arrangements are, little is known about how and when politicians compensate religious leaders for their electoral brokerage. We argue that politicians reward organization-embedded religious brokers by providing status-enhancing goods that increase their standing within the organization and the local community. We illustrate this type of compensation by investigating exchanges between Christian Democratic politicians and personally connected Catholic bishops in postwar Italy. Difference-in-differences estimates indicate that elected politicians reward connected bishops with investments in church renovations, that these investments are targeted to increase the prestige of bishops, and that electoral incentives shape patterns of broker compensation. These findings shed light on the reciprocal exchanges that underpin politician-clergy alliances in electoral democracies.

articles.title: The Spread of High-Speed Internet and Gender-Based Violence within Families in Mexico
articles.authors: Daniela R. Urbina, Julia A Behrman
articles.abstract: The relationship between internet access and gender-based violence (GBV) remains contested: theories of global diffusion sustain that online media spreads gender-egalitarian norms and condemns violence against women, whereas digital platforms can also normalize misogyny and enable coercive control. To test these hypotheses, we exploit temporal and geographic variation in the rollout of high-speed internet across Mexican municipalities between 2011 and 2021, distinguishing violence by intimate partners from that by other family members. Combining three waves of Mexico’s ENDIREH survey, with time-varying georeferenced coverage measures, we estimate two-way fixed-effects, difference-in-differences, and triple-difference models. We find that rapid internet expansion reduced family-perpetrated violence—particularly emotional and physical violence —but had no effect on intimate-partner violence. Further analyses reveal that one pathway through which increased digital access decreased family-level GBV was by enhancing women’s decision-making power, especially among those living with their parents. Our findings highlight the value of adopting a broad definition of GBV that reaches beyond intimate partners, particularly in contexts where multigenerational households are common.

articles.title: Resistance to territorial stigmatization: the mechanisms linking place-based social movement engagement and people's perceptions of place
articles.abstract: Scholars of territorial stigma have assumed that resistance efforts should improve how stigmatized neighborhoods are perceived. Findings from a two-and-a-half-year ethnographic study of a place-based social movement in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, challenge this assumption: the same organization's resistance efforts can produce fundamentally different effects depending on how audiences are positioned to encounter the neighborhood. For those with little direct contact, a consistent counternarrative reshaped how the neighborhood was symbolically imagined. For occasional visitors, direct exposure introduced complexity that secondhand accounts could not provide. For residents who engaged deeply with the organization, material and relational support gradually reshaped how the neighborhood was experienced from within. And for residents with high neighborhood familiarity but low organizational engagement, none of these mechanisms took hold. These findings reveal that resistance to territorial stigma and perception change are distinct processes, connected by mechanisms that vary with the nature and depth of contact between people and place, which shows how inequality is reproduced not only through material conditions but also through unequal processes of knowing place.

articles.title: What Citizens Mean by Democracy: Partisan Differences in Open-Ended Survey Responses
articles.authors: Mirko Wegemann, Elena Leuschner, Tim Lars Allinger, Daniel Bischof, Kristian Frederiksen, Morgan Le Corre Juratic
articles.abstract: Do voters from different partisan camps understand democracy in the same way? We analyze more than 25,000 open-ended survey responses from representative samples in 14 countries, classifying answers with a fine-tuned language model and sentence embeddings. Citizens most often define democracy through individual and civil rights; multidimensional definitions are rare, and elections are mentioned by only 17% of respondents. Yet shared vocabulary masks partisan divergence. Far-right voters and non-voters are less likely to mention civil rights, elections, and horizontal accountability, while far-right voters more often invoke majoritarian principles. Among respondents mentioning rights, left voters connect rights to equality and citizenship, whereas right voters emphasize freedom of speech. Democratic contestation thus unfolds within democratic language, creating openings for selective elite reframing.

articles.title: The impact of product placement on sales of plant-based meat alternatives: A controlled interrupted time series analysis of an in-store intervention
articles.authors: Alice Kininmonth, Francesca Pontin, Victoria Jenneson, William Young, Alison Fildes, Michelle Morris
articles.abstract: Background: Reducing meat consumption and substituting red and processed meats with plant-proteins could have positive health and environmental impacts. This study examined the impact of an in-store product positioning intervention on sales of plant-based meat alternatives (PBMA) and meat-based products. Methods: Between September 2021 and January 2022, a major UK supermarket retailer implemented a product placement intervention that moved 25 chilled PBMAs from a separate dedicated PBMA bay within the meat aisle to being shelved next to their meat-based counterparts and the original dedicated PBMA bay was removed. No changes were made in control stores. To examine the effectiveness of the intervention on sales of PBMAs and meat-based products, controlled interrupted time series analysis was conducted using 538 days of sales data from 6 intervention stores and 6 matched control stores. Results: Overall, there was a significant difference between intervention and control stores in the change in sales of PBMAs attributable to the intervention (-51.18 units, 95% CI: -97.15, -5.21, indicating that positioning PBMAs next to their meat-based counterparts led to a measurable reduction in PBMA sales in intervention stores. There was no difference between the intervention and control stores in sales of other meat-free products, meat-based products, or products within the protein Eatwell category, indicating that the intervention had no measurable effect on sales of products other than the relocated PBMAs. Price-point comparison analysis revealed that PBMA products were significantly more expensive than their meat-based counterparts. Conclusion: This study revealed that positioning PBMAs next to their meat-based counterparts was not effective at increasing sales of PBMAs and in fact led to a significant reduction in sales of the repositioned PBMAs. The reduction observed may have resulted from regular PBMA customers not being able to find the relocated PBMAs or from the higher price of PBMAs compared to their meat-based counterparts or both. Future research in real-world settings is needed to better understand the behavioural levers that encourage customers towards healthier and more sustainable purchases. Future research should also examine whether placement-based interventions, such as dual-placement coupled with price promotions, can support meaningful behavioural shifts towards more sustainable choices.

articles.title: Communication Repertoires in Hybrid Office Work: Mediated Channels, Face-to-Face Interaction, and Formal and Informal Exchange
articles.authors: Kai-David Klärner, Sophie-Charlotte Meyer, Anita Tisch
articles.abstract: Research on communication in hybrid work often focuses on individual channels or remote work intensity rather than the broader communication repertoires through which employees interact. This study examines whether the composition of these repertoires is associated with formal and informal collegial exchange beyond employees’ overall communication frequency. Using data from the 2024 DiWaBe 2.0 survey of 7,587 employees, we distinguish overall work-related communication frequency from its distribution across face-to-face interaction and four mediated channels: email, chat, telephone, and video conferencing. A joint five-mode model separates overall communication frequency from mode-specific deviations rela-tive to face-to-face interaction. Parallel measures enable a direct comparison of formal and informal exchange. The findings suggest that greater relative reliance on mediated channels is associated with lower reported formal and informal collegial exchange relative to face-to-face interaction. By contrast, voice/video and text-based channels do not differ significantly in their average associations with either outcome. The mediated-channel deviations also do not differ significantly between formal and informal exchange. Robustness analyses yield sub-stantively similar results across alternative samples, additional controls, and model specifications. The study demonstrates the analytical value of a communication-repertoire perspective on hybrid work. Overall communication frequency and communication-mode composition represent distinct dimensions of employees’ communication repertoires. The findings therefore shift attention from workplace location or individual channels alone to how communication is organised across co-present and mediated forms.

articles.title: Epistemic Intolerance Toward Outpartisans
articles.authors: Seo-young Silvia Kim, Taegyoon Kim, Jeong Hyun Kim, Youngdeuk Park
articles.abstract: We identify and operationalize epistemic intolerance, the belief that outgroup members are epistemically incompetent, violate epistemic norms, and are unworthy of epistemic engagement. In particular, we measure epistemic intolerance toward outpartisans using an original 18-item battery fielded in two U.S. surveys (December 2025 and April 2026; N = 3,386, of whom 2,525 partisans are analyzed). We show that epistemic intolerance is widespread and distinct from affective polarization and that, when measured with the full battery, it predicts democratic norm erosion, outparty dehumanization, and anti-intellectualism toward outparty elites, even when benchmarked against both affective polarization and political sectarianism. Moreover, its overall level is bipartisan, and prevalent even among leaners across both the Democratic and Republican parties. These findings identify epistemic intolerance as a consequential and previously underappreciated dimension of partisan hostility, with downstream implications for designing effective depolarization strategies.

articles.title: Barriers to disclosing school-based sexual harassment for racially-minoritised girls in the UK
articles.authors: Vanita Sundaram, Beth Bell, Nadia Jessop, Emma Jackson
articles.abstract: Abstract This paper focuses on barriers to disclosing school-based sexual harassment for racially-minoritised girls in the UK. The data are derived from the first UK study of racially minoritised girls’ experiences of public sexual harassment; in this paper we focus specifically on sexual harassment experiences in school. We adopted a qualitative research design that used co-produced, participatory methods to elicit the voices of racially-minoritised girls and young women. Twenty-eight participants from schools, community settings, and universities took part in semi-structured interviews and focus groups that used techniques such as photo elicitation and creative methods to prompt discussion. Barriers to disclosure fall into four thematic categories: feeling dismissed; lack of appropriate adults to disclose to in school; normalisation of sexual harassment; and victim-blaming. The findings make an important contribution to the scant UK literature on the school-level experiences of racially minoritised girls and demonstrate how race/ethnicity shape these experiences. Keywords: sexual harassment, schools, disclosure, barriers, racially-minoritised girls

articles.title: Affordable Health Advice: Rethinking Credibility in Digital Health Communication
articles.abstract: This Global Forum article proposes “affordable health advice” as a complementary lens for understanding credibility and livability in digital health communication. Drawing on my previous research on Egyptian physician vloggers and using a recent Egyptian digital health controversy as an illustrative thread, the article argues that audiences do not evaluate health advice only through scientific validity, source expertise, trust, or health literacy. They may also assess whether advice appears possible to live with. The article identifies three dimensions of affordability: economic, cultural, and emotional. Economic affordability concerns whether advice appears financially attainable and sustainable in contexts where treatment, medication, testing, food, and long-term disease management impose substantial costs. Cultural affordability concerns whether advice speaks from within people’s everyday language, food practices, religious rhythms, humor, and classed realities. Emotional affordability concerns whether advice reduces the psychological burden of illness by promising hope, autonomy, and relief from chronic-patient identity. The article argues that health advice may gain credibility when it appears more compatible with lived realities than conventional recommendations, even when that advice is scientifically contested.

articles.title: Cultural constructions of nature connection: Exploring migrants' experiences of connecting with nature in Australia
articles.authors: Kate Sollis, Bethaney Turner, Lily van Eeden, Kanchana Wiset, Usitha Rajeevan, Pauline Marsh, Emily Flies

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Cultural norms and values influence human-nature connection, shaping then how people use, and interact with natural environments and their nature stewardship actions. This study examines how nature connection varies across migrant communities in Australia and explores the role of cultural factors in shaping human–nature relationships. Using a mixed-methods approach, we analyse data from a national survey of 4,006 respondents in Australia, exploring the quantitative measures (CN-12 and Inclusion of Nature in Self) and qualitative responses from the respondents born overseas. Migrants reported higher overall nature connection than non-migrants, with particularly high levels among individuals from North African and Middle Eastern, Southern and Central Asian, Southern and Eastern European, and Sub-Saharan African backgrounds. However, differences in connection were not explained by socio-demographic factors, migration history, or access to nature. Qualitative findings reveal distinct conceptualisations of nature, including everyday interactions, human–nature entanglement, recognition of nature’s agency, reciprocity, and experiences of awe. These findings suggest that both cultural values and lived experiences shape how nature is understood and engaged with, highlighting the need for culturally inclusive approaches to environmental policy and nature-based interventions.

articles.title: Democracy, a Sine Qua Non Tool for Economic Development: The Ghanaian Experience (1950–2022)
articles.abstract: At independence in 1957, Ghana’s per capita income was comparable to South Korea’s, yet decades later the two countries occupy vastly different positions in the global economy. What explains this divergence, and what role has democratic governance played in Ghana’s economic trajectory? This study investigates the relationship between democracy and economic development in Ghana from 1950 to 2022, a period marked by cycles of military rule, economic decline, and democratic transition. While the existing literature extensively debates whether democracy causes development or development enables democracy, far less attention has been given to testing this relationship within a single-country time series that spans both authoritarian and democratic eras. I argue that democratic consolidation in Ghana has had a positive and statistically significant effect on economic growth. Using data from the Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) dataset and a bivariate regression model with GDP as the dependent variable and the V-Dem democracy index as the independent variable, the analysis reveals that a one-unit increase in democratic quality corresponds to a 2.056-unit increase in GDP, with democracy explaining approximately 41.6% of the observed variation in economic output.

articles.title: Properly Initiated: Gangstalking, Targeted Individuals and Digital Cults of Affliction.
articles.abstract: Targeted Individuals (TIs) describe “gangstalking” as coordinated, technologically mediated persecution that profoundly restructures everyday life. While clinical frameworks often interpret these experiences as individual delusion, such approaches overlook their collective and ritual dimensions. Drawing on digital ethnography, multi-platform participant observation, and interviews with TIs, this article reframes online TI communities through Victor Turner’s concept of cults of affliction. I argue that these networks function as contemporary curative cults, guiding participants through a tripartite rite of passage: separation, liminal seclusion, and return. Within this process, influencers act as modern diviners, transforming isolated sufferers into “wounded healers” who diagnose hidden enemies, construct therapeutic narratives, and perform public acts of revelation across digital platforms. This analysis positions gangstalking as a cultural concept of distress and a collective strategy for meaning-making, challenging medicalized models of mental illness and expert authority.

articles.title: Beyond the Billiard Ball: Understanding the Effectiveness of Transnational Politics
articles.abstract: This paper examines the conditions under which transnational political activity translates into measurable shifts in state behavior and the international order. Drawing on the foundational scholarship of Nye and Keohane (1971), Kaiser (1971), Keck and Sikkink (1998), Risse-Kappen (1995), and Vertovec (2009), I argue that the effectiveness of cross-border politics depends not on the existence of transnational actors alone but on the structured conditions through which they operate. The paper identifies persistent gaps in the existing literature, particularly the absence of systematic frameworks for assessing when transnational pressure yields tangible policy outcomes versus symbolic compliance. To address this, I propose the Layered Mediation Framework (LMF), a five-layer sequential model that evaluates transnational effectiveness through political openness, domestic institutional pathways, advocacy and accountability networks, the strength of issue framing, and the policy-to-actualization gap. The LMF offers a comparative analytical tool for measuring the flow, mediation, and ultimate impact of transnational political activity across different cases and regimes.

articles.title: How Do Benjamin Barber and Iris Young Seek to Create Justice?
articles.abstract: This paper examines how Benjamin Barber and Iris Marion Young seek to create justice through democratic reform. Both theorists reject the adequacy of liberal democratic institutions and advocate for deeper, more inclusive forms of public deliberation. Young proposes a transformative approach centered on remedying internal and external exclusions through institutional reform, group representation, and expanded modes of communication—greeting, rhetoric, and narrative— that foster dialogical understanding. Barber advances a more radical vision, calling for the replacement of existing “thin democratic” institutions with new participatory structures, including neighborhood assemblies, election by lot, national referenda, and universal citizen service. The paper identifies significant convergences between the two theorists, particularly their shared emphasis on diverse communicative practices, civic education, and the pursuit of a common will over parochial interests. It also highlights key divergences: Young favors reforming existing institutions to be more representative, while Barber argues such institutions are fundamentally flawed and must be replaced entirely. The paper concludes that Young’s incremental, reform oriented approach offers a more pragmatic and implementable pathway to democratic justice.

articles.title: Between Multifactor and Multi-Beta
articles.abstract: Given extensive evidence that firm characteristics predict expected returns, much of the literature asks whether these characteristics also capture the covariance structure of returns. If so, the next question is which modeling framework best explains the covariance structure revealed by those characteristics. This study addresses that question by comparing two alternative frameworks: a multifactor model and a conditional single-factor model. It formally examines how each specifies the covariance structure and how much overall return covariation each explains. The analysis then considers whether the covariance structure implied by the multifactor model can be nested within the conditional single-factor model.

articles.title: An Algorithmic Multifactor Extension
articles.abstract: Anomaly-based multifactor models have become a major development in empirical asset pricing because they provide a systematic way to expand existing pricing models. This study clarifies the algorithmic logic behind that extension. Specifically, it shows how these models identify pricing errors left unexplained by the factors already included in a model and incorporate additional factors to reduce those errors. This logic matters because it explains how anomaly-based models absorb empirical anomalies while reducing dimensionality. We further show that the method for adding factors closely parallels a classical factor-extraction algorithm in statistical modeling, thereby reinforcing the statistical validity of anomaly-based models.

articles.title: Informational Limits behind the Puzzle
articles.abstract: Some level of consumption is indispensable for survival. Human well-being, however, depends not only on present consumption but also on the expectation that consumption can be sustained in the future. Traditional economic models do not fully capture this forward-looking psychological dimension. This study revises the standard utility specification by incorporating expectation-based satisfaction. It also recognizes that consumers predict their own future consumption better than researchers do. Because utility depends directly on these private predictions, informational asymmetry matters for empirical asset pricing. The study shows how accounting for this asymmetry can help explain empirically high equity premia and low risk-free rates.

articles.title: Shared Governance in Hospitals: Development, Frameworks, and Future Directions for Interprofessional Implementation and Evaluation
articles.authors: Christoph Golz, Kai-Uwe Schmitt, Mirjam Körner
articles.abstract: Shared governance has been recognized for more than three decades as an organizational framework for strengthening nurses’ participation in decision-making, professional autonomy, and accountability. In recent years, the concept has regained attention as healthcare organizations face workforce shortages, increasing care complexity, and growing demands for interprofessional collaboration. This Expert Opinion examines the development, implementation, and evaluation of shared governance from nursing-centered models toward broader professional and interprofessional governance systems. Building on existing conceptual and measurement work, it discusses the conditions under which shared governance can be translated consistently into an explicit interprofessional decision-making system, with clearly defined authority, alignment with existing structures, and robust evaluation. Implementation is complicated by conceptual overlap with frameworks such as the Magnet model, distributed leadership, clinical governance, quality improvement structures, and interprofessional collaboration. These overlaps may blur responsibilities, duplicate structures, and complicate the attribution of outcomes to shared governance. Measurement approaches have advanced but remain fragmented. Instruments such as the Index of Professional (Nursing) Governance and the Verran Professional Governance Scale assess perceptions of governance culture, while the Council Health Survey provides a council-level measure of council functioning. However, current measurement approaches do not yet sufficiently capture interprofessional governance as an operational system, including how authority is distributed across professional groups, how decisions move through organizational structures, and how governance contributes to workforce, patient, and organizational outcomes. We propose a research and practice agenda that emphasizes conceptual clarification, interprofessional alignment with existing organizational frameworks, measurement innovation, and rigorous implementation and evaluation designs. Future work should combine measures of governance culture, council functioning, interprofessional representation, decision pathways, structural characteristics, and outcomes. Such an approach can help shared governance move from symbolic or fragmented implementation toward a measurable and sustainable mechanism for strengthening professional engagement, workforce retention, interprofessional collaboration, and the quality and safety of patient care.

articles.title: Risks and possibilities in sharing preprints during the doctorate
articles.abstract: During doctoral candidature, students may seek to publish journal articles, which they may incorporate in their thesis if their institutional policy permits. They may consider sharing pre-prints of these texts either pre- or post-publication to promote open access and knowledge mobilisation. There is very little extant research that explores doctoral students’ knowledge of the risks and possibilities involved in sharing their work in this form, and this chapter seeks to identify those that they could encounter. It offers immediate value for informing doctoral education and a useful foundation for future research that is specific to the doctoral student experience.

articles.title: International Migration: A Barrier towards Help Seeking for IPV among South Asian Immigrant Women in the US
articles.abstract: The literature review explores the way international migration works as the barrier in seeking help by South Asian immigrant women in the U.S. Significant number of women from these countries experience IPV and suffers from asking for help or support due to different aspects of South Asian culture. This review examines the structural barriers faced by these populations and also, looked into the theoretical perspective of fundamental cause theory. Finally, the review addressed the future scope of study and need for culturally driven services targeted toward these women.

articles.title: Agent-oriented modality in the languages of North America
articles.authors: Jessica K. Ivani, Alexandra Nogina, Taras Zakharko
articles.abstract: This study examines the morphosyntactic and functional encoding of agent-oriented modality in a maximally diverse sample of languages from North America. Focusing on necessity, obligation, ability, and desire, we show that agent-oriented modality is expressed through a wide range of construction types, including tense-aspect-mood morphology, modal verbs, non-verbal formatives, and complex clauses. We show that clustering the constructions by their formal properties yields three groups that align closely with the modal functions of necessity, ability, and desire. We further show that the constructions encoding different modal functions tend to differ in their morphosyntactic profiles, with strong necessity and obligation in particular showing systematic associations with tense marking, and weak and strong necessity with mood marking, respectively. These findings suggest that agent-oriented modality is not a uniform grammatical category, but a structured functional domain whose subtypes recruit material from different areas of grammar. The study contributes to a typological understanding of modality by combining constructional detail and an autotypologizing approach to cross-linguistic comparison.

articles.title: Embodied Knowledge: The Case of Sociology
articles.abstract: Spontaneous Community Research (SCR)—research that draws on experiences accumulated over years or decades of community participation before research questions are formulated—generates valuable sociological knowledge from insider perspectives. Yet current ethical frameworks and journal data requirements often exclude this approach. This article demonstrates that standard expectations—such as prospective research design, informed consent, tangible data deposits, and reproducibility—are incompatible with SCR's distinctive characteristics because its data are embodied: stored in the researcher's memory, inseparable from lived experience, and not amenable to conventional documentation. Rather than excluding SCR from academic discourse, the article argues for epistemic pluralism by recognising multiple legitimate forms of social knowledge production, each requiring ethical standards that are appropriate to its methodology rather than uniformly applied. To this end, it proposes alternative validation strategies that emphasise contextual transparency, collective corroboration, and reflexive acknowledgement of the evolution of the researcher's positionality. Keywords: embodied knowledge, insider research, autoethnography, positionality, data repositories, research ethics

articles.title: BLACK LGBTI+ PENTECOSTAL FAMILIES AND AFFECT OF RESISTANCE: DECOLONIAL PERSPECTIVES FROM THE BRAZILIAN PERIPHERY
articles.abstract: This paper presents key results from doctoral research in Religious Studies on Black LGBTI+ Pentecostal families in Brazil, conceptualized herein as quilombo families (famílias aquilombadas), viewed as ethical-affective expressions of resistance within the religious field. Utilizing an intersectional, decolonial, and affective framework, engaging critical scholars such as Joe Coyle, E. Patrick Johnson, and Beatriz Nascimento, the study deploys the metaphor of the Pentecostal quilombo to analyze inclusive churches as urban territories of affection, freedom, and the restoration of social bonds. Grounded in semi-structured qualitative interviews with 33 Black LGBTI+ individuals and families across inclusive congregations, the findings reveal how these family units challenge traditional Christian heterocisnormative dogmas and articulate a counter-hegemonic spirituality. This framework demonstrates both the transformative potential of affective-political reconstruction and the structural limits of inclusion when racial, moral, and gender hierarchies remain unbroken.

articles.title: LABRASHURIAS: THE PRETOGAYS LANGUAGE OF PENTECOSTAL INCLUSIVE CHURCHES
articles.abstract: The "pretogays" language (Santos, 2022) represents a linguistic manifestation resulting from the intersection of the epistemic category "pretoguês" (Gonzalez, 1988), the vernacular "pajubá" (Lima, 2017), a "dialect" of "resistance" utilized by transvestites and transgender individuals, and "glossolalia" (Sullivan, 2020), the characteristic and mystical speech of Pentecostals. These three communicative modes converge among LGBTI+ individuals within inclusive Pentecostal churches in Brazil, faith communities that do not condemn dissident sexualities but reframe them as divine gifts. Utilizing an intersectional framework (Crenshaw, 2002), further enriched by E. Patrick Johnson's Quare theory, Ashon Crawley's Blackpentecostal Breath, and Black sociolinguistics (Smitherman; Alim), this study demonstrates how race, class, gender, linguistics, and religion intersect to reveal how words and speech acts function as performative signs intrinsically linked to Black, gay, and Pentecostal embodiment.

articles.title: Dual Momentum: Cash Flows and Discount Rates
articles.abstract: Observed continuation in abnormal returns is best understood not as a primitive phenomenon, but as the combined effect of two channels: cash-flow momentum and discount-rate momentum. This two-channel view follows directly from the identity that decomposes abnormal returns into cash-flow news and discount-rate news. We show that these channels imply distinct patterns in the joint behavior of raw returns and normal returns, extending the analysis beyond the canonical facts of momentum. These patterns provide a diagnostic for assessing whether momentum profits are driven more by cash-flow momentum or by discount-rate momentum.

articles.title: Intertemporal Dynamics of Asset Prices
articles.abstract: A basic intuition in asset pricing is that higher perceived risk is associated with higher expected return. Yet this intuition alone does not fully explain how expected return is translated into realized return. An important link is therefore still missing. To address that gap, this study moves beyond the static risk-return tradeoff and focuses on three intertemporal elements: information processing, repricing in response to revisions in perceived risk, and hedging against future reinvestment risk. By bringing these elements together, the study explains how asset prices evolve over time and how returns take shape over time.

articles.title: Speculation-Based Asset Pricing
articles.abstract: This study proposes speculation-based asset pricing, in which valuation is driven by speculative beliefs and return forecasts rather than by risk-based dividend discounting. This shift matters because the theory does not require a dividend stream and therefore applies to non-dividend-paying assets. The key object is a speculative baseline return, defined as the return level investors believe the asset can eventually deliver. This baseline determines the explosive growth rate of the bubble component, which identifies the speculative part of the asset price. The analysis then shows a dynamic implication: faster convergence to this growth potential requires a greater near-term return cost.

articles.title: Institutions and the future African fertility decline
articles.abstract: Africa will account for nearly all global population growth in the 21st century, driven by persistently high fertility rates and substantial demographic momentum. This paper argues that, while many of the distal factors that affect fertility (for example, education, urbanisation, and contraceptive access) are well-understood as important determinants of fertility patterns and levels, demographers have tended to focus on these at the expense of considering the less-quantifiable institutional aspects which mediate the impact of those factors on the pace and timing of fertility declines. Drawing on McNicoll's foundational framework, we argue that weak, contested, or unstable institutions render high fertility a rational household strategy. Without deliberate institution-building — analogous to East Asia's developmental states — a demographic-institutional trap is likely to perpetuate Africa's elevated fertility well into the 21st century.

articles.title: Bringing public attention to disease into global health priority-setting
articles.authors: Wenceslao Arroyo-Machado, Ismael Rafols, Adrian A. Díaz-Faes

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Background: A central concern in global health priority-setting is whether the supply of scientific knowledge aligns with health needs and demands. This alignment is usually assessed by comparing research effort with disease burden, overlooking other type of “social demand” of disease, in particular whether diseases are socially visible and generate public attention. We develop an analytical framework that treats public attention and epidemiological burden as complementary dimensions of health demand and examines their alignment with knowledge supply. Methods: We combine data on publications indexed in OpenAlex, disability-adjusted life years from the Global Burden of Disease, and Wikipedia pageviews for 2016 to 2023, as indicators of research effort, disease burden, and public attention, respectively. We map 19 disease groups and 138 specific diseases across these three dimensions. Ternary plots are used to position diseases according to their relative balance across dimensions and to identify diseases that are over- or under-represented in research effort relative to epidemiological burden and public attention. We compare Global North-South patterns using German, Persian, Swahili, and Vietnamese language areas to assess how these relationships vary across territories. Results: The three dimensions show limited alignment. At the disease group level, cardiovascular diseases account for the largest share of disease burden, mental disorders attract the largest share of public attention, and neoplasms concentrate the largest share of research effort. Public attention and disease burden are weakly correlated at both group and specific disease levels, indicating that Wikipedia pageviews and DALYs capture distinct dimensions of health demand. Ternary plots reveal different forms of misalignment, with some diseases showing plots dominated by burden, others by research effort, and others by public attention. Territorial analyses add a further layer by showing that diseases follow disparate patterns of supply-demand (mis)alignment across different linguistic territories. Conclusions: Public attention provides a complementary dimension for mapping global health needs and demands. Our approach identifies where scientific knowledge supply fails to match epidemiological and/or public attention, supporting more nuanced global health analysis that may be useful for priority-setting.

articles.title: Examining communicative disenfranchisement and the commercialization of perimenopause and menopause on TikTok and Instagram
