articles.abstract: Menopause has a contested and complex history as evidenced by cultural representations of women’s health, shifting scientific recommendations for treatment, and challenges with diagnosing this life transition. Women increasingly report experiences with disenfranchised talk, including being silenced, discredited, and stereotyped, all of which prevent timely diagnosis and treatment. Social media has recently commercialized perimenopause and menopause, which contributes to greater confusion. Sensitized by the Theory of Communicative Disenfranchisement, we used content analysis to examine Instagram (n=135) and TikTok (n=134) content about perimenopause and menopause. We document a focus on symptoms, management strategies, commercialization, and disenfranchised talk and its consequences. Practical and theoretical implications for applying TCD in mediated spaces that consider commercialization and self-gaslighting, as well as creating authentic content to reach audiences interested in this life transition, are provided.

articles.title: Formal Improvement and Further Research on Classificatory Kinship Systems (Part 1)
articles.abstract: Abstract ：Social organization and kinship systems are major subjects of study in social anthropology. For over a century, this research has faced considerable challenges, primarily due to the immaturity of formal representations. Formal representations of kinship serve as tools for cognition and logical deduction, much like mathematics is to physics. In many cases, the quality of these formalrepresentations directly determines the accuracy of our understanding of the subject. The quality standards are maximum completeness, accuracy, intuitiveness, and simplicity, facilitating understanding, memorization, and use. This paper focuses on the intermarriage and succession rules of the Australian Kariera type, a system that was once widespread in the early social formations of various peoples around the world. This paper is divided into two parts. The first part, building upon previous research, presents a complete set of formal representation rules (symbols, formulas, and diagrams); it also provides over twenty Australian ethnographic cases (4 Category System and four groups of intermarriage and succession formulas) to demonstrate the verifiability of the formal representations presented in this paper. Based on this, it provides two types of (patrilineal and matrilineal) kinship tracing and derivation tools, illustrated with diagrams. The Kariera case, employing the instrumental diagrams presented in this paper, positively analyzes the 4 Category System kinship system, thereby further demonstrating the instrumental quality of the formal representation presented in this paper. Based on this, the generation process of Classificatory kinship System relationships is discussed.The issue of "double descent" in the Kariera system is a century-old problem, which this paper addresses through a formalized explanation. The conclusion briefly summarizes the composition of the Classificatory kinship System.

articles.title: Predictability in Strategic Asset Allocation
articles.abstract: The benchmark chosen under strategic asset allocation serves as the fund’s long-term target, while the actual portfolio composition fluctuates around that target over time. When active managers adjust portfolio weights in response to forecasts of benchmark returns, return predictability becomes valuable because it creates opportunities for effective short-term tactical adjustment. Predictability therefore enters utility as a distinct source of benefit. This role of predictability is not captured by the traditional mean-variance framework. The study therefore extends that framework by introducing predictability directly into the analysis. The resulting mean-variance-predictability framework defines the benchmark choice problem and reshapes the associated pricing relation.

articles.title: Price Dynamics and Investor Mobility
articles.abstract: This study develops an equilibrium framework for asset price dynamics under heterogeneous investor beliefs. It shows that price changes admit three equivalent representations, each linked to a distinct channel: group dominance, order imbalance, and participation tilt. As an application of the third representation, the study introduces investor mobility as a measure of how actively investors shift their participation across belief groups over time. Higher mobility indicates greater changes in investor composition and, for a given level of forecast dispersion, larger price movements. The study implements this concept empirically by constructing and analyzing a market-wide series of investor mobility.

articles.title: Seeing Amsterdam through Google Maps: Uneven visibility and crowd-based mapping

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: How is the city represented and shaped through Google Maps? Through a computational analysis of over 106,000 places in Amsterdam, this paper examines how Google Maps represents and creates urban hierarchies and differences. Drawing on critical cartography and platform studies, we examine how Google Maps’ affordances and modes of crowd-sourced data collection generate uneven platform geographies: consumption-oriented places, scenes, and neighbourhoods stand out while others are pushed to the background. However, we also show that Google Maps intervenes into processes of segregation and gentrification in complex ways; we do not find straightforward platform-promoted displacement. Through a granular analysis of one street, we show that there are synergistic connections between places that may seem to be in competition and that different communities use Google Maps to appraise the street in culturally specific ways. Both our city-wide and street-level analyses demonstrate that Google Maps functions as a constitutive urban infrastructure that creates platform geographies by spawning hierarchies of visibility and marking differences.

articles.title: The City Multiple: Comparing Geographies of Digital Visibility across Google Maps, Instagram, Facebook, and TikTok
articles.abstract: Digital platforms have become key geospatial infrastructures through which cities are discovered, experienced, and evaluated. Whereas the extant literature has often focused on single platforms or assumed an undifferentiated platform urbanism, we know very little about how different platforms produce distinct geographies of urban visibility. To address this lacuna, we examine the spatially differentiated regimes of visibility that emerge when platforms mediate urban environments. In doing so, we distinguish between three dimensions of platforms’ geographies of digital visibility: (1) spatial inequality—how each platform distributes visibility across places; (2) spatial articulation—how platform visibilities map onto local urban geographies; and (3) spatial representation—the kinds of places and content that achieve visibility on each platform. Combining computational, geographic, and interpretive methods, we analyse how 6,682 eating and drinking establishments in Amsterdam are represented on TikTok, Instagram, Google Maps, and Facebook, and find strikingly weak correlations between their visibility on the four platforms. We find that each platform produces distinct structures of unequal visibility, with algorithmic-discovery platforms concentrating visibility more intensely than review-based systems. Neighbourhood-level analyses further show that platform-specific spatial articulations correspond to the gentrification and touristification of specific areas. Our findings contribute to the literatures on digital geography and platform urbanism by demonstrating that digital platforms generate multiple instantiations of the same city.

articles.title: The affective bases of socialized preferences
articles.abstract: Research on family socialization suggests that the drivers of preferences (such as values and attitudes) are rooted in early life experiences. But the cognitive process that connects past experiences to present thought processes is not well understood or theorized. In this article, I draw on recent cognitive science research on the role of affectively-valenced memories in shaping preferences, and the sensitivity of the involved cognitive processes to top-of-mind concerns. Revisiting socialization theories in light of these ideas suggests that while rooted in affective memories, socialized preferences are results of probabilistic predictions of the brain and are malleable to priming. Across 3 related studies, including a preregistered survey experiment, I examine the empirical case of socialization of inclinations towards parenthood.

articles.title: One Policy, Many Publics: Central Bank Communication and the National Politics of Trust

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Central bank decisions have become politically contested. In response, central banks communicate more with the public, since their effectiveness rests on public trust. Yet whether they reach ordinary citizens is largely unknown. We exploit the European Central Bank’s unexpected announcement of the Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme (PEPP) during the fieldwork of a March 2020 survey in Germany and Italy. Our results show that the same decisive intervention was rewarded only where it aligned with the perceived national interest: in Italy, trust in the ECB rose, strongest among news-followers and the left; in Germany, trust in the ECB did not move at all, even as trust in national institutions surged. Preferences for central bank goal independence moved in neither country. Citizens thus notice exceptional monetary policy decisions, but their responses are mediated by national interests and discourses, with asymmetric consequences for a central bank that makes one policy for many publics.

articles.title: Legal Threats and Online Dissent: Evidence from Social Media Regulation in Turkey
articles.authors: Arvind Magesan, Juan S. Morales, Arieda Muço
articles.abstract: We study how legal threats to social media platforms shape online political communication. We exploit the sharp implementation of a 2020 Turkish law that required social media companies to establish local offices and provide user data to the government on request. Assembling a panel of over 700 Twitter users and 7 million posts, we use a differences-in-differences design to compare dissenters, individuals publicly critical of the reform when announced, to other groups unlikely to be affected, such as celebrities. We find that dissenters and political exiles post 15-20 percent fewer tweets following implementation, and engagement with their content falls sharply. These short-run chilling effects emerge despite limited platform compliance, indicating that anticipated enforcement risk, rather than actual enforcement, drives the effect. In the long run, the chilling effects dissipate. Our findings suggest that states can govern online speech indirectly, by regulating platforms rather than users, but that such effects may be self-limiting in the absence of visible enforcement.

articles.title: Children’s Art Experiences: Interactive Digital Art
articles.authors: Emilie Bossens, Bieke Zaman, Priscilla Van Even
articles.abstract: Art invites exploratory, multisensory, emotionally rich and context-shaped forms of engagement, yet these experiences are sometimes difficult to capture. This challenge becomes especially pronounced with children, whose meaning-making relies on movement, sensation and play, rather than verbal reflection or evaluative judgements. Because most cultural spaces are designed around adult norms and expectations, children’s distinctive ways of engaging with art often remain overlooked or under supported. This raises questions about how cultural settings can better accommodate what children themselves experience as meaningful aesthetic encounters. In this chapter, we first review research on children’s art engagement from perceptual, cognitive, emotional, bodily, spatial, and social perspectives. We then present a case-study of 215 children aged 3 to 12 years old engaging with an interactive digital artwork at a family arts festival. Through systematic observations, we identify three recurring interaction patterns, demonstrate how social dynamics and contextual factors shape children’s unfolding engagement, and show how children exert agency through their exploratory actions and the artwork’s responsive features. Building on these insights, the chapter concludes with future directions for art research and practice, calling for child-centered methodologies, stronger attention to embodiment and emotion, and closer art-science collaboration to better support meaningful art experiences for children.

articles.title: Rural-Urban Differences in Student Journalism Performance Metrics
articles.abstract: This paper examines rural-urban differences in student journalism performance among higher education institution (HEI) student produced news outlets. With journalism quality frameworks, three article-level dimensions serve as comparisons: textual distinctiveness, Critical Information Needs (CIN) coverage, and localeness. Using a dataset of approximately 15,000 student articles, we utilized outlet-level soft cosine similarity, validated LLM-assisted binary coding, and logistic regression. Our results suggest three findings within our dataset: 1) the textual patterns of articles are not strongly structured by locale, 2) rural articles had substantially higher descriptive rates and odds of addressing a CIN than urban articles, and 3) rural articles had higher descriptive rates and odds of being coded as local. These results suggest that student journalism’s local-news role varies more in their civic ability, corroborating that being locally engaged is not synchronous with addressing CINs and that rural-urban differences could extend beyond institutional capacities into HEIs informational role in surrounding communities.

articles.title: Aid Cuts and the Politics of Refugee Hosting
articles.abstract: In 2025, U.S. aid cuts drove the fastest contraction of foreign aid on record. These cuts threaten the cooperative arrangement underpinning the refugee regime, in which low- and middle-income countries host most refugees while high-income countries finance assistance. As host communities lose aid-related jobs, services, and infrastructure, does citizens’ willingness to host refugees decline? I examine this question in Kenya using two nationwide surveys, a high-frequency panel and vignette experiment near Kakuma camp, and 52 interviews with local leaders, all conducted as the cuts unfolded. Support for hosting declined in refugee- hosting areas as economic losses and insecurity grew, driven by households that lost camp-based benefits. By contrast, national support remained stable, and exploratory evidence suggests that humanitarian concern limited backlash. Yet because refugee policy often responds to pressures in hosting regions, continued cuts may weaken the local foundations of asylum in the countries that host most of the world’s refugees.

articles.title: Chaotic Dynamics of Asset Prices
articles.abstract: This study offers a new perspective on asset price dynamics by showing that seemingly irregular price movements are governed by a common structure. It separates the forces underlying these movements and develops three equivalent representations that make this structure more transparent. A central construct in the study is a time-varying parameter that classifies price dynamics into interpretable regimes. In the empirical analysis of aggregate stock prices, periods of higher parameter values, indicating more turbulent regimes, align closely with major economic downturns. This evidence supports the parameter’s use as a diagnostic tool for detecting regime shifts and periods of macro-financial turbulence.

articles.title: Arbitrage-Induced Mispricing
articles.abstract: Contrary to common belief, arbitrageurs and mean-variance optimizers are not direct counterparts in trading. Their portfolio positions may instead overlap, amplifying fluctuations in aggregate demand for assets with particular positioning signals and pushing prices away from fundamental values. These deviations, in turn, create additional hedging demand. This study examines whether overlap in position setting between arbitrageurs and mean-variance optimizers generates mispricing and whether this mispricing becomes a priced source of risk. The empirical findings support both possibilities: they confirm the presence of such mispricing and show that additional pricing factors are needed to account for it.

articles.title: Climate Adaptation as Evolvability
articles.authors: Michael Weisberg, Rachael Brown, Christopher H. Lean

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Standard approaches to climate adaptation, commonly understood as the protection of infrastructure, social systems, and ecosystems from adverse climate impacts,are too closely tied to the biological concept of adaptation and the ecological notion of stability. Instead, we argue that climate adaptation is better articulated by analogy to the concept of evolvability. Adaptation thus understood emphasizes the need for internal capacities of restoration and self-maintenance, preserves flexibility and options for the future, addresses the social, political, and psychological impacts of climate change, and promotes transboundary strategies.

articles.title: A Contract-Based Healthcare Ecosystem for Depopulated Rural Communities: Residential Risk Visibility and Incentive-Linked Health Monitoring

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Debates on healthcare sustainability in depopulated rural communities have focused on technological solutions — telemedicine, drone delivery, remote monitoring. This paper addresses the structural problems technology alone cannot solve: helicopter emergency medical services (HEMS) cannot fly at night or in bad weather; severe emergencies admit no alternative to physical transport; and the healthcare costs generated by rural residence remain invisible to both residents and society. We propose a "contract-based healthcare ecosystem": (a) quantifying and visualizing the relationship between residence location and medical access as individual risk; (b) making participation in continuous health monitoring a contractual condition of new residency; and (c) linking participation and risk-management attainment to basic-income-style payments. On ethical grounds the scheme applies only to new residents, with existing residents guaranteed conventional arrangements. Extending the external-balance model of our companion paper (SocArXiv, doi:10.31235/osf.io/rcsq9_v1), we estimate that if 60 high-risk residents of a 500-person community participate in monitoring and severe events fall by 15-35%, incentive payments of 2,500-11,700 yen per person per month are offset by reduced external medical expenditure alone (break-even). This range is realistic for behavior-change incentives, implying that a scheme in which health-risk management directly contributes to community economic self-sufficiency is institutionally feasible. Ethical limits concerning privacy, stigmatization, and freedom of choice are examined from a clinician's perspective. Note: The full manuscript is written in Japanese; an English abstract is provided above.

articles.title: Testing the water: Importance of surface water resources for settlement installation in various climatic contexts using a machine learning approach
articles.abstract: Past human spatial dynamics are strongly influenced by water availability. Since the development of agrarian sedentary societies, water is seen as an essential ressource. Yet quantifying its influence on past populations across different environmental and chronological contexts remains methodologically challenging. This study investigates the relative importance of thirteen water-related variables alongside five additional environmental covariates in shaping archaeological site distributions. Using machine learning model of Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt), a total of 461 Bronze Age and Iron Age (3,500 - 50 BCE) sites from four regions with contrasting climatic conditions - the Rhine Valley, Lazio, the Shephelah, and the Kurdistan region of Iraq - were analysed. Results show that distance to water flow and stable topographic variables consistently emerge as the strongest predictors of settlement location. Palaeoclimatic variables, particularly precipitation seasonality and precipitation of the wettest quarter, outperform modern remote sensing indices. Despite contrasting environmental conditions, the four regions share broadly comparable settlement trajectories, with a consistent shift toward greater site density and spatial dispersion from the Bronze Age to the Iron Age. These findings highlight the value of temporally robust environmental proxies for modelling past human-landscape interactions and offer a replicable framework for water-focused archaeological predictive modelling across diverse climatic settings.

articles.title: Constitution-Making After Contested Elections: The Constitutional Legitimacy Threshold and Tanzania’s Post-2025 Reform Dilemma
articles.abstract: Constitution-making after contested elections presents a fundamental dilemma for democratic governance: whether institutions whose own legitimacy is disputed can credibly undertake the task of creating a new constitutional order. This article examines Tanzania’s post-2025 constitutional reform debate through the concept of the constitutional legitimacy threshold, arguing that constitution-making requires a higher level of legitimacy than ordinary legislative governance (Beetham, 1991; Habermas, 1996). Drawing on theories of constituent power and constitutional authority (Sieyès, 1789; Ackerman, 1991), the article distinguishes between formal constitutional competence and substantive constitutional legitimacy. While Tanzania’s Parliament may possess legal authority to initiate constitutional reform under existing constitutional procedures, the article argues that foundational constitutional transformation requires broader conditions of representative credibility, political inclusion, and public confidence (Elster, 1995; Arato, 2016). Using Tanzania as a case study, the article analyses how electoral contestation, institutional distrust, and political polarization affect the legitimacy of constitution-making processes. It demonstrates that disputed electoral mandates can generate a gap between the legal authority of institutions and their capacity to produce a constitutional settlement accepted across society. The analysis draws on comparative constitutional experiences to show that durable constitutional orders are frequently associated with inclusive participation, negotiated legitimacy, and broad societal ownership (Klug, 2000; Ghai & Cottrell, 2010). The article contributes to comparative constitutional politics by developing the constitutional legitimacy threshold as an analytical framework for understanding why some constitution-making processes achieve durability while others remain contested. It argues that successful constitutional reform depends not only on procedural legality but also on the perceived legitimacy of the institutions, actors, and processes responsible for producing the constitutional order. The Tanzanian case illustrates a broader challenge facing emerging democracies: constitutional renewal requires not merely the power to change constitutional rules, but the legitimacy necessary to establish rules that command enduring acceptance.

articles.title: Why Play When AI Can Win: The Non-Transferability of Participation in AI-Assisted Play
articles.abstract: Knowledge work is learning to hand itself over. Drafting, analysis, computation, even the role of a practice opponent can now be delegated to artificial intelligence, and the delegation works: the results come back, often better and faster than one's own. This paper asks what, in that handover, does not move. Drawing on Bernard Suits's analysis of games, I separate the achieved state of an activity from the value of participating in it and defend a non-transferability theorem: parts of an activity can be delegated, but no agent, human or artificial, can take over one's participation itself. When another realises the goal state on my behalf, the fact that I undertook the constitutive constraints and pursued the goal through them does not thereby come into existence. AI can deliver the state of affairs; it cannot deliver the fact of participation. At bottom, then, the central claim is not a claim about AI at all: the theorem is agent-relative, and holds whatever machines become — achievers, players, moral patients, or none of these. What it leaves open is the human question. Whether one can keep playing, lucidly, in full knowledge of the machine's strength, depends not only on individual temperament but on whether a culture grants dignity to those who do unnecessary things in earnest. Japanese professional shogi, which met machine superiority a decade ahead of other knowledge domains and kept its play, is examined as a completed historical case — public evidence that the question in this paper's title has already been answered, once, in the affirmative.

articles.title: Coding choices and short-sequence artefacts undermine claims of a conventional Palaeolithic sign system – a comment on Bentz and Dutkiewicz (2026)
articles.abstract: In this comment, I show that methodological and statistical flaws undermine the central conclusions of Bentz and Dutkiewicz (2026).

articles.title: Reskilling and Retraining the Water Technology Workforce: An Agentic Generative AI Framework for Water Purification, Nano‑MEMS, and Curriculum Development
articles.abstract: The rapid digitalization of water infrastructure is bringing artificial intelligence, advanced sensing, and membrane materials science into routine water treatment practice. At the same time, utilities, regulators, and training institutions face a persistent workforce challenge: many operators, engineers, and managers are being asked to adopt data-driven tools without a coherent educational pathway that links AI literacy to real treatment workflows. This article synthesizes recent literature on agentic generative AI, reinforcement learning, smart sensing, nano-enabled membranes, and digital twins for water systems, then translates those developments into a structured reskilling model for the water sector. The proposed framework is organized around three competency tiers: foundational AI and data literacy for water professionals; applied agentic AI for decision support, process optimization, and predictive maintenance; and advanced nano-AI integration for sensor-rich treatment trains, membrane design, and digitally enabled R&D. The manuscript further proposes journal-ready tables covering competency architecture, course design, and implementation priorities, alongside conceptual figures illustrating the interaction between water purification processes, AI agents, nano-MEMS monitoring, governance, and workforce outcomes. Rather than treating automation as a substitute for expertise, the framework positions human-in-the-loop supervision, risk management, interoperability, and regulatory compliance as core curriculum requirements. The article argues that reskilling should be embedded in utility modernization strategies, community-college pipelines, professional certificates, and utility-academic partnerships so that adoption of smart water purification systems is matched by operator trust, safety assurance, and practical competence.

articles.title: Digital Infrastructures and Contemporary Governance in Times of Conflict
articles.abstract: Scholarship on internet shutdowns and digital authoritarianism tends to treat digital infrastructure as an instrument of repression, while research on wartime digital government treats it as an instrument of resilience. This article argues that the two are not separable: in conditions of acute interstate war, the same architecture can simultaneously secure a regime’s continuity and restrict the visibility of its population. Drawing on Michael Mann’s concept of infrastructural power and using the 2026 U.S.–Israel–Iran war as a revealing single case, it examines connectivity control, command decentralization, cyber pressure on critical systems, and the management of online narratives as one governing logic rather than discrete tactics. A central claim is that wartime decentralization mattered politically as well as militarily: it helped preserve authority after leadership losses and communications disruption, while the same distributed architecture widened the scope for miscalculation and escalation. The article’s contribution is to specify a mechanism the two literatures have tended to treat separately — the co-location of resilience and repression in a single infrastructure, and the double-edged character of the decentralization that sustains continuity.

articles.title: Economic Constitutionalism: Legitimate Authority and the Democratic Governance of Institutional Purpose

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Formally accountable regulation can remain inadequate when its objectives are privately, technically, or distributionally insulated from democratic authorization. This article introduces economic constitutionalism as a second-order framework that extends regulatory legitimacy analysis from the conduct of regulators to the authority to define what regulation is for. The analysis reconstructs authorization assumptions across regulatory legitimacy, capture, public-purpose, and quantification literatures and derives three mechanisms of regulatory-purpose displacement and four design properties for purpose-responsive regulation. Applications to artificial intelligence, platform labor, education, care, and public information demonstrate the framework's comparative diagnostic reach. The argument shifts the regulatory design agenda from procedural compliance alone to the authorization and revision of regulatory purpose.

articles.title: Fuzzy Cross-Database Record Matching for Missing and Unidentified Person Cases: Design and Retrospective Validation of the CAIRN Engine
articles.abstract: Abstract Missing-person (MP) and unidentified-person (UID) records in the United States are fragmented across federal, state, county, and volunteer-maintained systems, and the matching applied within those systems is predominantly exact-field or manual. This paper describes CAIRN (Case Analysis and Intelligent Resolution Network), a hypothesis-generation engine that scores MP-UID candidate pairs using seven weighted, error- tolerant signals (fuzzy name similarity, distinguishing marks, temporal compatibility, geographic distance, age fit, height/weight, and race with subset tolerance), applies two hard filters that eliminate a pair outright rather than scoring it (biological sex, and chronological impossibility), and attaches an explicit confidence tier reflecting how many identity-grade signals supported each score. The engine was validated retrospectively on forty-eight confirmed-solved case pairs assembled from Internet Archive snapshots of Doe Network case pages, current NamUs records, official press materials, and recovered snapshots of NamUs records deleted after resolution. In a ranking benchmark on six solved pairs that took four to forty-two years to resolve in reality - decades combined - the engine ranked the true match first in six of six cases in a matter of seconds. Forty-two additional pairs spanning records-strong, minimal-data, recovered- record, and movement and concealment classes scored between 0.463 and 1.000, each consistent with its evidentiary class. Of the twelve pairs scoring above 0.92, ten required more than a year of human review to connect and five required more than a decade, with a median of approximately three years; the two exceptions, resolved in roughly one month and roughly nine months respectively, are the two most recent cases in the benchmark. Two confirmed matches are eliminated outright by hard filters: one by an incorrectly recorded biological sex, and one by a missing-person report date standing in for a last-contact date, placing the recovery twenty years before the reported disappearance. A separate prospective field test cross-scored 2,508 Florida MP and 869 Florida UID summary records, measuring behaviour under summary-level data rather than match accuracy. It demonstrated that summary- level data alone produces high-scoring but low-confidence false positives; all three top-ranked candidates were disproven under human review, and the failures directly motivated three engine corrections now incorporated. All output is framed as leads for human verification through official channels, never as conclusions.

articles.title: Identifiability limits in rare network count processes: a simulation laboratory with empirical probes in crime, seismology and neural spike trains
articles.abstract: Rare network count data — panels with 90–99% zeros across nodes and time — are common in criminology, seismology and neuroscience, where a fitted Poisson, negative-binomial or zero-inflated model is often read as evidence about mechanism. Using a simulation laboratory of ten stress-test data-generating processes and semi-synthetic probes in UK Police, USGS and Allen Neuropixels data, this work shows that model fingerprints, dispersion, residual autocorrelation and intervention estimates can instead reflect sparsity, the observation operator and effect design. Identifiability is layered: a stable fingerprint is not a mechanism.
